Portable Power Station for RV: Sizing and What It Runs 
 Skip to content 
 A portable power station can run an RV’s everyday loads (fridge, lights, internet, laptops) for a day or more: our example day uses about 1,600 Wh , so plan on roughly 2,250 Wh per day between recharges. The air conditioner is the hard part: a standard 13,500 Btu rooftop unit draws up to about 1,860 VA, which empties a 2,048 Wh station in under an hour of compressor time. A station’s 30-amp RV outlet only delivers what its inverter is rated for, so check the watts, not the plug.

 An RV already has its own electrical system: a 12V house battery, a converter that charges it, and a shore power cord for campground hookups. A portable power station doesn’t replace that system. It works as a second, movable source: a quiet substitute for a generator when you camp without hookups. This guide covers how much it can do, with the math shown.
 How a power station connects to an RV
 There are two plug-and-play ways to use one, and neither involves wiring:
 Plug devices straight into the station. This is the most efficient option for a laptop, a coffee maker or a CPAP.
 Plug the RV’s shore power cord into the station. The RV then behaves as if it were on a (small) campground hookup, and its outlets work. Some stations have a NEMA TT-30 outlet, the same 30-amp socket found on campground pedestals, so a 30-amp RV cord fits without an adapter.
 Two things to know when the whole RV is plugged into the station:
 Your converter will try to charge the house battery from the station. That moves energy from one battery to another with losses along the way. Check your RV’s manual for how to switch the converter or charger off while you’re on the station.
 Everything left on in the RV counts. A water heater on electric mode or an air conditioner left on auto can drain the station while you’re away.
 Safety: Use the RV’s own shore power cord, and only adapters approved for that use. Never use a cord with two male ends, and never connect a power station to the RV’s wiring or panel yourself: permanent connections, transfer switches and alternator chargers are jobs for a qualified RV technician or electrician. If you also carry a fuel generator, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission warns never to run one inside or near an enclosed space; keep it outdoors, at least 20 feet away, with the exhaust pointed away from the RV. Carbon monoxide can kill in minutes.
 What “30 amp” really means
 A 30-amp RV hookup is 120 volts × 30 amps = 3,600 watts . A 50-amp hookup has two 50-amp, 120-volt lines, up to 12,000 watts . A power station with a TT-30 outlet does not automatically deliver 3,600 W: the limit is its inverter.

Weight matters in an RV: whatever the station weighs comes out of your cargo carrying capacity.
 Can it run the RV air conditioner?
 Sometimes, and not for long. Dometic’s installation manual for its rooftop units lists these figures for the FreshJet 3 13,500 Btu model (FJX3473M), at 115 V:
 Compressor: 13.6 A rated; fan: 2.6 A rated. Together, 16.2 A × 115 V = about 1,860 VA while the compressor runs. (Volt-amps are what the inverter has to supply; the real watts are somewhat lower.)
 Compressor locked-rotor current: 71 A. That’s the momentary worst case at startup, about 8,165 VA.
 Minimum generator size: 3.5 kW for one unit, according to Dometic’s general guideline.
 Those numbers set two tests for a power station.
 1. Can it start the compressor? Compare the station’s surge rating with that startup current, and treat Dometic’s 3.5 kW generator guideline as a warning: a station rated well below that may not start a standard unit at all. Ask the station’s manufacturer about your air conditioner model before you count on it.
 2. How long can it run it? Using the same formula as our runtime calculator :
 runtime (h) = battery Wh × 0.85 ÷ load 
 2,048 Wh station: 2,048 × 0.85 ÷ 1,860 = about 0.9 hours of compressor time
 4,096 Wh station: 4,096 × 0.85 ÷ 1,860 = about 1.9 hours of compressor time
 These are hours with the compressor running , calculated from rated current, so they are a conservative floor. The compressor cycles on and off, and how often depends on the heat, the sun and your RV’s insulation, so real hours of cooling will be longer. We don’t have a published figure for that, so we don’t estimate it.
 A more efficient air conditioner changes the picture. The same Dometic manual lists the FreshJet 5 high-efficiency model (FJX5357MHE) at 8.8 A for the compressor and 3.6 A for the fan: about 1,430 VA , with a locked-rotor current of 55 A. That gives about 1.2 hours on 2,048 Wh and 2.4 hours on 4,096 Wh.
 The practical conclusion: a power station can cool the RV for a lunch stop or take the edge off before bed. For air conditioning all afternoon without hookups, you need a much larger battery bank or a generator. Our battery vs gas generator comparison covers that trade-off.

 Without the air conditioner, the numbers are friendly. Here is an example day with the RV plugged into the station:

 Portable panels have one real advantage in an RV: you can park in the shade and put the panels in the sun , angled toward it. Panels mounted flat on the roof can’t be aimed, and in winter that costs a lot: in Phoenix in December, a flat panel receives about 57% of what an angled one does (3.18 vs 5.53 peak sun hours). Check the station’s solar input limits before buying panels: the two stations above accept up to 1,200 W and 2,600 W.
 Other ways to recharge on the road
 For charging times and the limits of each method, see How to Charge a Portable Power Station .
 Campground hookups: on a night with shore power, the station recharges from an outlet like it does at home. The AC200L, for example, lists up to 2,400 W of AC input.
 Driving: many stations can charge from a vehicle’s 12V outlet; check the manual for the rate, which is usually modest. Faster alternator chargers exist, but they are wired into the vehicle and should be installed by a professional.
 A generator, during allowed hours: many campgrounds restrict generator use. Our camping guide has an example of those rules. One option is to run a generator during the allowed hours to refill the station, and use the station in silence the rest of the day.

How to Choose a Portable Power Station for a 30-Amp RV | WattMatch 
 August 16, 2026 · 15 min read · Overlanding 
 How to Choose a Portable Power Station for a 30-Amp RV
 Many RV owners shop by battery capacity first, then discover that a large battery does not automatically solve air-conditioner startup, 30-amp shore-power limits, or awkward outlet connections. The right question is not simply how many watt-hours (Wh) the station has, but which RV loads it can start, how long it can run them, and whether a standard 30-amp shore cord plugs in directly. This guide turns those constraints into a practical buying decision.
 Choosing a portable power station for 30-amp RV use starts with the RV’s actual loads, not the biggest capacity in watt-hours (Wh). A 30-amp, 120V connection represents 3,600W on paper, but an air-conditioner compressor starting alongside a microwave, coffee maker, or charger can consume that margin quickly.
 This guide is for motorhome and travel-trailer owners who want selected 120V appliances during RV boondocking without installing a permanent electrical system. It covers startup output, usable runtime, solar recovery, carrying weight, and the outlet that actually matches a 30-amp shore cord: NEMA TT-30R.
 Free tool No signup 
 Runtime
 Estimate your runtime
 Enter your RV appliances and expected hours into WattMatch's runtime calculator, then compare the high-output RV-ready stations to see which option meets your load without carrying more battery than you can use.

 Quick take
 Start with the 3,600W ceiling: A 30-amp, 120V RV connection cannot use a station’s full 6,000W or 4,000W rating through that connection.
 Treat air conditioning as two separate problems: The station must handle compressor startup, then have enough battery capacity to run the unit for the time you need.
 Match the plug, not the marketing: A standard 30-amp RV shore cord is TT-30. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3, Anker SOLIX F3000, and BLUETTI Apex 300 have built-in TT-30R outlets. The Anker SOLIX F3800 uses NEMA 14-50 and L14-30, so a typical 30-amp cord needs an adapter.
 Do not overvalue surge output: A high surge number does not confirm that a particular RV air conditioner will start, because the appliance’s startup requirement and the surge duration both matter.
 Plan to recharge: Solar input and AC recharge speed determine whether the station can recover between appliance use, driving days, or campsite stops.
 Start with what a 30-amp RV can actually use
 The basic calculation is simple:
 120V × 30A = 3,600W 
 That is the theoretical shore-power ceiling for a 30-amp RV connection. It is not a recommendation to run 3,600W continuously without checking the coach, appliance combination, and station setup. It is the upper limit that frames the decision.
 A portable station rated above 3,600W is still useful. The RV’s 30-amp breaker and cord remain the continuous ceiling, but compressor startup is a brief spike. Breakers are built to hold through short inrush, so the station’s inverter has to supply that same spike. If the inverter’s continuous rating is already 3,600W, any overlapping load or heat-related derating leaves the station as the weak link even when its surge number looks large. Extra continuous headroom on the F3800 (6,000W) and DELTA Pro 3 (4,000W) is there for that moment. It does not turn a 30-amp shore cord into a 50-amp system.
 This is also where 120V/240V marketing can distract from the real question. Most of the loads in this scenario are 120V RV appliances. Native 240V capability is useful for other applications, but it does not automatically improve the amount of power available through a 30-amp RV connection.
 Air conditioning is the difficult load
 An RV air conditioner combines a demanding startup event with potentially long runtime. The compressor may require more power to start than it uses after reaching operating speed. At the same time, the refrigerator controls, lights, fans, chargers, and other appliances continue drawing power.
 Before buying, find the air conditioner’s running wattage and its starting requirement from the nameplate, manual, or manufacturer. If that information is unavailable, a power station’s surge rating alone is not enough to promise compatibility.
 The four stations have these headline AC ratings:
 Power station Continuous AC output Surge output Battery capacity 
 Anker SOLIX F3800 6,000W 9,000W 3,840Wh 
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 4,000W 8,000W 4,096Wh 
 BLUETTI Apex 300 3,840W 7,680W 2,764.8Wh 
 Anker SOLIX F3000 3,600W 7,200W 3,072Wh host

 The F3800 has the most continuous output headroom, but that does not guarantee that it will start every RV air conditioner. The specific compressor requirement still decides that. The F3000 matches the theoretical 30-amp ceiling exactly, leaving no extra continuous margin for overlapping loads. The DELTA Pro 3 and Apex 300 sit only modestly above that ceiling.
 EcoFlow’s supplied description cites a 3-ton central air-conditioner example under controlled conditions with a soft starter. That is not proof that the DELTA Pro 3 will start a particular RV air conditioner. Treat that example as a reminder that startup equipment and operating conditions can change the result.
 Runtime depends on watts, not just Wh
 The basic runtime estimate is:
 Runtime in hours ≈ battery capacity in Wh ÷ actual load in watts 
 That calculation is only a starting point. It does not account for inverter losses, reserve capacity, changing compressor demand, or other appliances running at the same time. Actual runtime will be lower than the simple division suggests.
 A 13,500 BTU RV air conditioner often runs in a roughly 1,200W to 1,800W band after it starts. Using 1,500W as a planning load, the nominal arithmetic looks like this:

 The F3000 needs a configuration note. Its host capacity is 3,072Wh, but the default listing described in the product data includes a BP3000 expansion battery for about 6,144Wh in the box before losses. Do not use the bundle total if you are comparing the standalone host.
 At a 3,600W load, even the larger batteries empty quickly in simple theoretical math. The F3800 works out to about 1.07 hours, the DELTA Pro 3 about 1.14 hours, the F3000 host about 0.85 hours, and the Apex 300 about 0.77 hours before losses. An air conditioner will not necessarily draw its rated maximum continuously, but these figures show why output capability and endurance must be evaluated separately.
 The RV connection can decide the purchase
 A station may have enough wattage and still be inconvenient to use if its outlet does not match the RV’s shore cord.
 A standard 30-amp RV shore cord is NEMA TT-30: 120V, 30A, three-prong. That is a different connector from NEMA 14-50 (the 50-amp RV / EV receptacle) and from NEMA L14-30 (a locking 120V/240V 30A receptacle common on generators and some home-backup gear). For plugging the coach’s 30-amp cord into the station, TT-30R is the direct fit.

 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 TT-30R, 120V/30A L14-30R and 6-20R in 240V mode Plugs in directly in 120V mode 
 Anker SOLIX F3000 TT-30R, 3,600W max NEMA 5-20R Plugs in directly 
 BLUETTI Apex 300 TT-30R, 3,600W max NEMA 14-50R Plugs in directly 
 Anker SOLIX F3800 None NEMA 14-50 and L14-30 Needs a dogbone or similar adapter 
 The DELTA Pro 3, F3000, and Apex 300 are the plug-and-play 30-amp options in this group: the RV shore cord goes into the station’s TT-30R without an adapter. Two caveats still matter. On the DELTA Pro 3, 120V and 240V outlet groups are not all live at once; turn on 120V AC so the TT-30R is powered. On the Apex 300, the TT-30R is capped at 3,600W even though the inverter is 3,840W.
 The F3800 is still an RV-oriented station, just not a native TT-30 station. Anker lists NEMA 14-50 and L14-30 for RV and EV use, which is a better native match for 50-amp inlets and some generator-style cables. A typical 30-amp shore cord will not plug into those receptacles without an adapter. Do not confuse this F3800 with the F3800 Plus, which Anker lists with a TT-30 outlet.
 Do not assume that a generic 5-20 household outlet is equivalent to a dedicated RV receptacle. At a campsite, a cord that seats correctly is more useful than a small increase in battery capacity.
 Solar input affects how long a weekend can last
 Solar input is the maximum charging power the station is designed to accept under the stated setup. It is not a guarantee that portable panels will deliver that amount in normal conditions.
 The listed solar inputs are:
 Anker SOLIX F3800: up to 2,400W
 Anker SOLIX F3000: up to 2,400W
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3: up to 2,600W across dual PV inputs
 BLUETTI Apex 300: 2,400W built-in; up to 4,000W with the SolarX 4K accessory
 The Apex 300’s higher figure is accessory-dependent, so it should not be compared directly with the built-in figure without confirming the complete charging setup. The practical question is how much energy you can recover during the daylight window, not just which station has the largest input ceiling.
 If the air conditioner uses more power than the panels provide, the battery still drains. Solar is most useful here as a recovery plan: reduce the battery deficit during the day, then reserve stored energy for evening loads or periods when the panels are not producing enough.
 Which stations fit this 30-amp RV use case?
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is the strongest overall 30-amp match when you want a native TT-30R, the largest base battery, and a little inverter room above 3,600W. It provides 4,096Wh of LiFePO4 storage, 4,000W of continuous AC output, and 8,000W of surge output. The built-in TT-30R is a direct fit for a 30-amp shore cord once the station is in 120V AC mode.
 That extra 400W of continuous output is useful, but it is not a dramatic increase and it does not authorize drawing more than the RV connection can support. Its 120V/240V output is valuable in broader backup use, while the up to 2,600W dual-PV input can help recover energy during a sunny boondocking day.
 EcoFlow markets 0–80% charging in about 50 minutes, and the product data describes UPS-style switching around 10ms. Those features matter more for fast recovery and sensitive electronics than for solving air-conditioner runtime. At about 113.5 lbs, it is substantial, though lighter than the F3800.

That is the largest output margin here for compressor startup and overlapping appliance loads, although the air conditioner’s actual startup requirement still needs to be checked.

 How to choose without overbuying
 Build a real load list
 Write down the appliances you actually expect to use:
 RV air conditioner
 Refrigerator controls
 Interior and exterior lights
 Microwave
 Coffee maker
 Phone, laptop, and other chargers
 Fans or other 120V equipment
 Record both running wattage and startup requirements where applicable. The most common mistake is adding only the running watts while ignoring the compressor or motor startup event.
 Also identify which appliances will run at the same time. A microwave used for three minutes may not consume much daily energy, but it can create a high instantaneous load when the air conditioner is already running.
 Decide whether you need the whole coach powered
 There are two different buying goals:
 A selected-load setup: You power individual appliances and electronics as needed.
 An RV-connection setup: You connect the station to the coach and let the RV’s existing circuits distribute power.
 The first approach can work with a smaller station if you are disciplined about which loads run together. The second makes outlet compatibility, grounding, the 30-amp ceiling, and load management much more important.
 If your main goal is occasional coffee, refrigeration controls, lights, and device charging, paying for the heaviest inverter available may not be necessary. If air conditioning through the coach is central to the plan, prioritize startup information and a TT-30R (or a known-good adapter plan) before chasing expansion capacity.
 Match battery size to the length of use
 Use the calculator for a more realistic estimate, but start with the formula:
 Required battery capacity ≈ total watts × hours of use 
 Then allow for inverter losses and the fact that appliance loads change over time. A station with 4,096Wh does not provide 4,096Wh of usable AC output at the appliances. It also does not mean an air conditioner will run for four hours unless the actual average load is close to 1,000W and the station’s conversion losses are ignored.
 For a weekend, consider the energy cycle rather than a single runtime number. How much will the RV consume overnight? How much will the air conditioner use during the hottest part of the day? Can solar recover enough energy before evening? Will driving provide another charging opportunity? Those questions usually produce a better purchase decision than comparing capacity alone.
 Check the connection before checking expansion
 Expansion batteries can solve a storage problem, but they do not solve an incompatible outlet or an output bottleneck. Confirm the RV inlet, the station’s supported outlet, and the manufacturer’s connection instructions first.
 For a standard 30-amp shore cord, the DELTA Pro 3, F3000, and Apex 300 already have the matching TT-30R. The F3800 needs an adapter from its 14-50 or L14-30 outlets. Resolve that path before the station arrives at the campsite, including any grounding or mode-switch steps the manufacturer requires.
 Be honest about weight
 These are heavy-duty power stations. The listed weights range from 83.8 lbs for the Apex 300 to 132.3 lbs for the F3800. The DELTA Pro 3 is about 113.5 lbs, and the F3000 host is 91.5 lbs.
 A lighter station is easier to position and store, but it generally comes with a smaller base battery in this group. A larger station can provide more output or runtime, but only if you can safely move and store it. For towable campers, the best unit may be the one that can be positioned without turning every setup into a lifting problem.
 FAQ
 How many watts does a 30-amp RV need?
 A 30-amp, 120V RV connection represents 3,600W on paper. That does not mean every RV should be paired with a 3,600W station and run at that level continuously. Startup surges and simultaneous loads reduce the practical margin, especially when an air conditioner is operating.
 Can a portable power station run an RV air conditioner?
 It may, but compatibility depends on the air conditioner’s startup requirement, running demand, station output, connection method, and available battery capacity. A large surge rating is helpful, but it is not a guarantee. Check the air conditioner’s requirements before treating any station as an air-conditioning solution.
 Is a 3,000Wh station enough for an RV weekend?
 It can be enough for selected loads, especially when air conditioning is limited and solar or driving provides recharge opportunities. It is not automatically enough for continuous air-conditioner use. The Anker SOLIX F3000 host has 3,072Wh, while the described default bundle has about 6,144Wh before losses, so configuration matters.
 Does 120V/240V output help a 30-amp RV?
 Most of the relevant 30-amp RV loads are 120V, so 240V capability does not by itself increase the power available through the RV’s 30-amp connection. It can make a station more flexible for other applications, but the RV connection and load limit still need to be respected.
 Can solar run the RV air conditioner all day?
 Only if solar production keeps up with the air conditioner and the other loads. The station’s solar input rating is a maximum charging figure, not a guarantee of real-time energy production. In practice, solar is better treated as a way to reduce battery drain and recover energy during daylight.
 Takeaway
 The right portable power station for 30-amp RV use depends on the job you are asking it to do. For a native TT-30R, the largest base battery, and a little room above 3,600W, the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is the strongest overall fit. The Anker SOLIX F3800 still has the most inverter headroom, provided you can handle 132.3 lbs and an adapter on a typical 30-amp shore cord. The Anker SOLIX F3000 is the direct 3,600W plug-and-play match, and it becomes more compelling in the described 6,144Wh bundle. The BLUETTI Apex 300 is the lightest native TT-30 option, but its smaller battery makes it better for selected loads than extended air-conditioner use.
 Start with the 3,600W 30-amp ceiling, verify compressor startup requirements, calculate runtime from actual watts, and confirm that the shore cord matches the station’s outlet before buying. A power station that fits those four constraints will be more useful than one chosen solely for its largest capacity or surge number.

 Overlanding power is not just camping with more gear. Once a 12V fridge, lights, and charging from the vehicle all enter the picture, battery size and recharge speed matter much more than marketing hype.

 Van life Best Portable Power Stations for Van Life Without a Hardwired Electrical System
 The common mistake is buying a van-life power station like it only needs to pass one appliance test. Real van use is a daily loop: the fridge runs overnight, the fan runs while you sleep, devices charge in waves, and the battery has to recover before the next evening. The best pick is not always the biggest unit—it is the one that balances usable watt-hours, recharge speed, weight, and safe placement inside a small van.

 What does 30 amp RV service mean?
 A standard 30 amp RV electrical service in North America uses 120V through a NEMA TT-30 connection.
 The theoretical maximum service is 120V multiplied by 30A, which comes to 3,600W.
 That does not mean your RV constantly consumes 3,600W. It means the shore-power connection can provide up to that electrical limit.
 Your actual consumption may be 300W, 800W, 1,500W, 2,500W, or another value entirely, depending on which appliances are operating.
 A 30A plug does not mean the battery provides 30A continuously
 This is one of the biggest buying mistakes in this category.
 A station can physically have a TT-30 receptacle while still having an inverter rated below 3,600W.

 So the TT-30 connection gives the RV owner a convenient physical connection. It does not increase the inverter to 3,600W.

 TT-30 vs household outlet

 That is one reason the DELTA Pro and AC200L stand out in the current WattCrate lineup.
 TT-30 is not a dryer outlet
 Do not confuse NEMA TT-30 with other 30A connectors.
 TT-30 is a 120V RV connection. Other 30A receptacles can use different voltages, different pin arrangements, and different applications.
 Do not force incompatible connectors together. Use equipment designed for the exact electrical connection you are making.

 How much power can a 30 amp RV use?
 The theoretical maximum is 120V multiplied by 30A, which comes to 3,600W. That is the total available service.
 An illustrative combination might include an air conditioner at 1,500W, a microwave at 1,300W, a refrigerator at 150W, and converter and electronics at 200W.
 That would total 3,150W before considering startup events.
 This is why RV owners sometimes trip a 30A pedestal breaker even when connected to normal campground shore power. Load management still matters.
 A 30A RV does not constantly consume 3,600W
 The 3,600W figure is the service ceiling.
 A normal RV might spend long periods drawing 200W, 400W, or 700W depending on what is running. Then a major appliance switches on and demand rises sharply.
 This is why battery capacity should be calculated from energy over time rather than from 30A multiplied by 120V for every hour of the day. Our portable power station watt-hours explained guide covers the difference between watts and watt-hours.

 Suppose the refrigerator cycles, the water pump runs for seconds at a time, the microwave runs for a few minutes, the lights draw very little, and Starlink stays on continuously.
 The average load across an entire day can be much lower than the instantaneous peak.

 Is 2kWh enough for a 30 amp RV?

 But battery capacity is not the same as maximum shore-power output.
 The DELTA 2 Max and AC200L both store 2,048Wh. The AC200L has the convenience of native TT-30, while the DELTA 2 Max provides the same broad battery and output class with different connection options.
 For an RV owner who does not need rooftop A/C for hours at a time, 2kWh can be an excellent starting point.
 Is 3.6kWh better for a 30 amp RV?
 For serious RV use, yes.
 The DELTA Pro's 3,600Wh battery provides substantially more usable energy, and its 3,600W normal output better matches the theoretical full power of 30A/120V shore service.
 That combination is why the DELTA Pro wins this guide.
 Can DELTA Pro power an entire 30 amp RV?
 Potentially, within its voltage, outlet, total output, and battery-capacity limits.
 A DELTA Pro can supply the RV through its native TT-30 connection.
 But powering the whole RV does not mean running every appliance simultaneously forever. The total normal load still needs to remain within the station's output, and battery energy still determines runtime.
 An air conditioner and microwave running together can consume a large percentage of the available inverter output.
 Can AC200L power an entire 30 amp RV?
 It can power the RV through its native TT-30 connection, but the important limit is 2,400W of total normal AC output.
 So although the shore cord can connect through TT-30, the RV does not suddenly gain a full 3,600W power budget.
 The owner must manage high-draw appliances more carefully. This deserves emphasis, because the connector can otherwise create a misleading impression.
 Can DELTA 2 Max power a 30A RV?
 Potentially, through an appropriate connection where supported.
 But the station's normal output remains 2,400W. A properly rated adapter or connection changes plug compatibility, not inverter capacity.
 An adapter does not turn the DELTA 2 Max into full 30A shore service.
 Can a 30 amp RV run air conditioning from a power station?
 Potentially, but RV rooftop A/C is one of the hardest battery loads there is.
 A conventional unit may draw around 1,300W to 1,800W while actively cooling, depending on the model, and compressor startup can also matter.
 That is what makes the DELTA Pro particularly attractive here. Its 3,600W normal output leaves more room for the refrigerator, lights, converter, and Starlink while the A/C runs.
 Our best portable power station for RV air conditioner guide covers rooftop A/C sizing, startup surge, and realistic cooling runtime in full.
 DELTA Pro with RV air conditioning
 Suppose an RV A/C draws 1,500W and other RV loads total 300W, for a combined 1,800W.
 The DELTA Pro's 3,600W normal inverter leaves substantial additional output margin.
 But battery runtime still matters. At an average total load of 1,800W, the DELTA Pro's 3,060Wh WattCrate usable-energy planning value represents less than two continuous hours.
 Real A/C cycling can extend elapsed clock time. There is no exact number of cooled hours to promise here.
 AC200L with RV air conditioning
 Suppose the A/C draws 1,500W and other active loads total 300W, for a combined 1,800W.
 That fits inside the AC200L's 2,400W of normal output. But only 600W of normal output margin remains.
 A microwave or coffee maker could easily push the system beyond normal output. Load management becomes important.
 30 amp RV plus microwave
 A microwave can be a major temporary load. Use the microwave's electrical input watts, not just its advertised cooking watts.
 Suppose the A/C draws 1,500W, the microwave input is 1,300W, and other loads total 200W. That is 3,000W combined.
 The DELTA Pro has much more room for this kind of overlap.
 The AC200L or DELTA 2 Max would require active load management, because 3,000W exceeds their 2,400W of normal output.
 Turn off the A/C before using another large appliance
 Load management is normal even on a 30A campground pedestal.
 An RV owner may choose not to run rooftop A/C, a microwave, electric water heating, and a coffee maker all at the same time.
 That same strategy can make a 2,400W power station much more useful.
 The physical RV service may be 30A. The battery station does not need to reproduce all 30A simultaneously if the owner actively manages loads.
 30 amp RV refrigerator
 RV refrigerators vary. Possible designs include compressor refrigerators, absorption refrigerators, and residential-style refrigerators.
 Electrical demand can therefore differ dramatically, and there is no single universal RV refrigerator wattage worth publishing.
 For compressor refrigerators, startup demand can also matter. Our refrigerator startup watts guide covers that, and our best portable power station for refrigerator and freezer guide covers longer cold-storage backup.
 30 amp RV plus Starlink
 Starlink is relatively easy compared with HVAC. Starlink Mini typically uses only tens of watts, which makes it a natural continuous communications load in an RV.
 The bigger battery cost comes from running it for many hours. At 40W for 12 hours, that is 480Wh.
 That is meaningful, but still far less than several hours of rooftop A/C. Our best portable power station for Starlink guide covers the wider Starlink hardware range.
 30 amp RV plus CPAP
 A CPAP is another relatively modest inverter load, but it commonly runs overnight.
 For boondocking, the RV battery budget may need to cover the refrigerator, Starlink, a CPAP, and lights through the same night.
 That combination can easily justify a 2kWh or 3.6kWh power station. Our best portable power station for CPAP guide covers overnight sizing in more detail.
 30 amp RV plus electric water heater
 Electric water heating can be a large load.
 If the RV has alternative heating modes, do not assume battery-electric operation is always the best energy strategy. Check the exact appliance.
 A large electric heating element can consume battery quickly. That is particularly important when air conditioning or cooking appliances are operating too.
 30 amp RV plus coffee maker
 A coffee maker may use around 1,000W or more during heating, depending on the model, and it normally runs for a relatively short period.
 That means it can have a large impact on instantaneous inverter demand but a modest impact on total daily watt-hours compared with an air conditioner.
 For a 2,400W station, it may be sensible to temporarily disable another major appliance while making coffee.
 Can a portable power station replace an RV generator?
 Sometimes.
 For quiet overnight camping, Starlink, a CPAP, the refrigerator, electronics, lighting, and occasional kitchen appliances, a large battery can be excellent.
 For continuous air conditioning, several days off-grid, large electrical cooking loads, or a trip with no solar or recharge source, a fuel generator can still be easier to replenish.
 The right answer depends on daily energy use, not just inverter watts. Our portable power station vs generator guide compares both sides.
 Why DELTA Pro is especially compelling as a generator alternative
 The DELTA Pro provides native TT-30, 3,600W of output, a 3.6kWh battery, expansion options, solar charging, and quiet battery operation.
 That makes it one of the closest matches in the WattCrate product universe to the experience of plugging an RV shore cord into a portable source.
 It still has finite battery energy. A generator can be refueled much faster than a depleted battery can always be recharged under poor solar conditions.
 Solar charging for a 30 amp RV
 Solar is particularly valuable for RV use because many loads repeat every day, including the refrigerator, Starlink, lights, electronics, and a CPAP.
 Without recharging, even a large battery eventually reaches zero. Solar can replace part of the energy used during the day.
 But do not compare panel watts directly with daily appliance watt-hours without considering time.
 Daily solar harvest depends on sunlight hours, panel angle, shade, weather, season, and charging losses. Our how to charge a power station with solar guide covers realistic daily harvest.
 DELTA Pro solar for RV use
 Current EcoFlow documentation lists substantial solar charging capability for the DELTA Pro.
 That can be valuable during boondocking, because the 3.6kWh battery can absorb a large amount of daytime energy and continue supplying the RV after sunset.
 A full daily recharge is not something to count on. Actual production varies.
 AC200L solar for RV use
 Current BLUETTI US documentation lists substantial solar capability for the AC200L.
 That makes it a strong option for 30A travel trailers, daytime solar charging, and smaller off-grid energy budgets.
 Again, native TT-30 convenience does not change the 2,400W inverter ceiling.
 DELTA 2 Max solar for RV use
 The DELTA 2 Max can also be a strong solar-supported RV battery.
 Its 2,048Wh capacity makes it large enough to store meaningful daytime solar energy.
 For an RV whose normal loads remain under 2,400W, it can be a very capable setup. Our best solar generator for RV guide covers the full solar-plus-battery RV picture.
 Is a native TT-30 outlet worth it?
 For a 30A RV owner, it can be extremely convenient.
 A native TT-30 provides direct physical compatibility, fewer adapters, cleaner cable management, and less confusion about outlet types.
 But it should never be used as the sole purchasing criterion. You still need to compare inverter output, battery capacity, solar, weight, expansion, and your actual RV loads.
 TT-30 vs adapter
 A properly rated adapter can allow some power stations to connect to an RV shore cord where the electrical configuration is supported.
 But the adapter does not increase inverter watts, outlet current limit, or battery capacity.
 A 2,400W station connected to a 30A RV through an appropriate adapter remains a 2,400W source. It is not a 3,600W source just because the RV's cord is rated for 30A.
 Never use an unsafe RV adapter
 Homemade adapters, modified plugs, defeated grounding, male-to-male cables, backfeeding, improvised neutral-ground bonding, and undersized extension cords all belong on the do-not-do list.
 Use appropriately rated equipment intended for the exact electrical connection, and follow the RV manufacturer, power-station manufacturer, and adapter manufacturer instructions.
 What about a 50 amp RV?
 A 50A RV is a different electrical architecture.
 A typical North American 50A RV service provides two 120V legs and can support far more total electrical power than a 30A service.
 It should not be treated as the same thing as a 30A RV with a bigger plug.
 A 50A RV can still use reduced-capacity portable power arrangements, but that requires a separate sizing discussion.
 30A RV vs 50A RV
 A 30A RV service uses 120V on one hot leg, for up to approximately 3,600W.
 A typical 50A RV service uses a 120/240V split-phase architecture with two 120V legs and a much higher total service capacity.
 Do not calculate a 50A RV as simply 120 multiplied by 50 and call that the entire service. The common 50A RV service architecture provides substantially more total capacity.
 What size battery does a 30 amp RV need?
 Use this broad planning hierarchy.
 30A RV battery sizing
 1 Around 500Wh for Starlink, CPAP, phones, and electronics 
 2 Around 1kWh for lighter overnight essentials 
 3 Around 2kWh for serious boondocking without continuous A/C 
 4 Around 3.6kWh for larger mixed loads and stronger A/C capability 
 5 More than 3.6kWh or regular recharging for multi-day RV living and substantial air-conditioning use 
 This is a planning hierarchy, not a universal rule.
 Is 1kWh enough for a 30 amp RV?
 It can be useful, but it does not reproduce full 30A shore power.
 A DELTA 2 or AC180 can provide power for a refrigerator, Starlink, lights, a CPAP, a TV, and chargers for meaningful periods depending on consumption.
 Air conditioning drains the battery much faster.
 Is 2kWh enough for weekend RVing?
 For many weekend RVers, yes.
 This is the strongest use case for the DELTA 2 Max and AC200L. A 2kWh battery can support normal RV essentials for several hours.
 With solar and sensible load management, it becomes much more useful. For continuous rooftop A/C, 2kWh is still limited.
 Is 3.6kWh enough for a 30 amp RV?
 It is significantly more capable.
 The DELTA Pro gives the RV owner the full 3,600W inverter class, native TT-30, and a 3.6kWh battery. That makes it the strongest single-station match in the WattCrate lineup.
 But 3.6kWh does not mean unlimited boondocking, all-day rooftop A/C, or multi-day operation without recharge. Energy still has to come from somewhere.
 Best 30 amp RV setup for weekend camping
 For a weekend where A/C use is limited and the fridge, Starlink, lights, and electronics run, the DELTA 2 Max or AC200L can be very attractive.
 The AC200L gets the advantage of native TT-30. The DELTA 2 Max gets the advantage of lower weight and the wider EcoFlow accessory ecosystem.
 Our best portable power station for camping guide covers tent camping, and our best solar generator for van life guide covers smaller mobile rigs.
 Best 30 amp RV setup for serious boondocking
 For longer periods, the DELTA Pro is the strongest base station.
 The reasons are 3.6kWh of storage, 3.6kW of output, native TT-30, an expansion ecosystem, and strong solar support.
 Best 30 amp RV setup with air conditioning
 For rooftop A/C, the DELTA Pro is the most comfortable choice in the current lineup.
 Its larger inverter provides more headroom for overlapping RV loads, and its larger battery improves runtime.
 But air conditioning can still consume several kilowatt-hours quickly. The dedicated RV A/C guide covers the detailed calculation.
 How to size a power station for a 30 amp RV
 Use this order.
 30A RV sizing process
 1 Confirm the RV uses 120V 30A TT-30 service 
 2 List essential RV appliances 
 3 Find their running watts 
 4 Identify compressor and motor startup loads 
 5 Calculate realistic simultaneous demand 
 6 Decide whether native TT-30 matters 
 7 Choose inverter output above the intended simultaneous load 
 8 Calculate daily watt-hours separately 
 9 Decide whether 2kWh or 3.6kWh is appropriate 
 10 Add A/C energy separately 
 11 Plan solar, vehicle, campground, or generator recharging 
 12 Use appropriately rated RV connection equipment 
 13 Test the system before relying on it while boondocking 
 Do not buy from the number 30A alone. The actual loads matter. Try our runtime calculator with your own appliance list.
 Common 30 amp RV power station mistakes
 The first mistake is assuming a TT-30 receptacle automatically provides 3,600W.
 The second is confusing connector rating with inverter output.
 The third is assuming the RV constantly consumes 30A.
 The fourth is buying from battery watt-hours alone.
 The fifth is buying from inverter watts alone.
 The sixth is assuming a physical adapter increases power.
 The seventh is trying to run A/C and a microwave together on a smaller station.
 The eighth is ignoring compressor startup.
 The ninth is expecting 2kWh to provide all-day A/C.
 The tenth is expecting the DELTA Pro to provide unlimited RV power.
 The eleventh is assuming 30A and 50A RV service are essentially the same.
 The twelfth is using unsafe or homemade adapters.
 The thirteenth is assuming solar panels produce their rated watts all day.
 The fourteenth is waiting until a remote campsite to test the setup.
 Avoid those mistakes and 30A RV battery sizing becomes much easier.
 Which one should you buy?
 Buy the EcoFlow DELTA Pro if you want the strongest overall portable power station for a 30 amp RV. Its combination of native TT-30, 3,600W of normal output, and a 3,600Wh battery is the cleanest match in WattCrate's current product lineup.
 Buy the BLUETTI AC200L if you want a smaller 2kWh system with a native TT-30 connection and can manage your RV within its 2,400W of normal output.
 Buy the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max if you want a strong EcoFlow 2kWh RV battery and do not require native full-power TT-30 functionality.
 Buy the DELTA 2 or AC180 for lighter RV electrical use.
 Use the AC70, RIVER 2 Max, and AC50B for targeted RV loads rather than as 30A shore-power replacements.

 Final recommendation
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro is the best portable power station for a 30 amp RV in WattCrate's current lineup.
 It is one of the rare cases where the product's electrical architecture lines up unusually well with the search query.
 A normal 30A RV connection represents 120V multiplied by 30A, or 3,600W. The DELTA Pro provides 3,600W of normal AC output and a native NEMA TT-30 RV receptacle.
 Its 3,600Wh battery also gives substantially more useful boondocking capacity than a normal 1kWh or 2kWh station.
 The BLUETTI AC200L is the strongest alternative because it also provides a native TT-30 connection. But remember that its total normal AC output is 2,400W. The TT-30 receptacle does not turn the AC200L into a 3,600W source.
 For a 30A RV owner who wants the closest portable-battery equivalent to the normal shore-power connection, the DELTA Pro is the strongest WattCrate choice.
 Final answer
 Choose the EcoFlow DELTA Pro if your priority is a true RV-focused portable power station with native TT-30, 3,600W of normal output, and 3,600Wh of battery capacity.
 Choose the BLUETTI AC200L if you want native TT-30 in a smaller 2kWh package and can keep simultaneous RV demand below its 2,400W of normal output.
 Choose the DELTA 2 Max when you want a strong 2kWh EcoFlow system and can use a properly rated supported RV connection while managing loads within 2,400W.
 Most importantly, a 30 amp plug and 30 amp service are not the same thing as 3,600W of available inverter power.
 Always verify the connector, the voltage, the normal inverter output, your simultaneous appliance watts, the battery watt-hours, and your recharging plan before buying.

What Size Generator for a 30 Amp RV? 30A and 50A Sizing 
 Skip to content 
 A 30-amp RV can draw at most 3,600 W (30 A × 120 V), so a generator rated around 3,000–3,600 W covers one rooftop air conditioner plus everyday loads. A 50-amp RV has two 120 V legs of 50 A each, up to 12,000 W, and needs a much larger generator to use it fully.
 Key facts 
 30-amp RV service: one 120 V feed, 30 A × 120 V = 3,600 W maximum.
 50-amp RV service: two 120 V feeds of 50 A each, about 12,000 W in total.
 A 13,500 BTU rooftop AC runs on about 1,500–1,700 W but can surge to about 2,800–3,500 W at start without a soft starter.
 Cummins calls 2,500–2,800 W a common minimum for 30-amp RVs with air conditioning, and 3,600 W a match for 30-amp shore power.
 Generator outlets made for RVs are the TT-30R (30 A) and 14-50R (50 A).
 What size generator do I need for a 30-amp RV? 
 The 30-amp hookup caps what your RV can draw: 30 amps at 120 volts is 3,600 watts, and the RV's main breaker trips above that. A generator in the 3,000–3,600 W range (rated, not just peak) can therefore supply almost everything a 30-amp rig can use. Cummins, which makes RV generators, says a 3,600 W generator gives you the same power as 30-amp shore power and that 2,500–2,800 W is often a workable minimum for 30-amp RVs with an air conditioner.
 Which end of that range you need depends on the rooftop AC and what else runs with it:
 AC plus small loads (lights, fans, TV, phone and laptop charging, the converter keeping batteries topped up): a generator whose maximum output covers the AC's start surge, about 3,000 W for a 13,500 BTU unit without a soft starter.
 AC plus a microwave or coffee maker at the same time: about 3,100 W of running load, which is close to the 3,600 W ceiling of the hookup itself. You need a generator that can sustain that, or you take turns.
 Worked example: 30-amp travel trailer
 Item Running watts Starting watts 
 Rooftop AC (13,500 BTU) 1,600 3,000 
 TV 80 none 
 6 LED lights 54 none 
 Laptop 50 none 
 Total 1,784 largest: 3,000 
 Using our standard method (all running watts plus the largest starting load), the peak is about 4,800 W. That is a cautious figure, because the AC's 3,000 W starting number already includes its own running draw. In practice, Micro-Air, a soft-starter maker, says a 13,500 BTU unit needs at least a 3,000 W generator without a soft starter, and a 15,000 BTU unit at least 4,000 W. Our generator size calculator will run the numbers for your own list.
 Turn on the microwave (about 1,500 W) while the AC runs and the running load climbs to about 3,300 W, near both the hookup limit and the rated output of a 3,000 W-class generator. Switch the AC off while you cook, or step up in size.
 What size generator do I need for a 50-amp RV? 
 A 50-amp RV plugs into a 14-50 receptacle that carries two separate 120 V legs, each able to supply 50 A. That is 6,000 W per leg and about 12,000 W in all. Cummins says a 12,000–12,500 W generator is the top end for a 50-amp RV and puts a Class A coach with three 15,000 BTU air conditioners at about 10,000–12,500 W.
 You don't have to match the full 12,000 W. Many 50-amp owners size for what they really run, for example two ACs plus a few kitchen items, and manage the rest. Work out your list the same way: add every running load, then the single largest starting load, and check that the generator has a 14-50R outlet or a matching hookup.
 The RV's breaker panel splits its circuits between the two legs. A generator connected through a 30-amp adapter feeds both legs from one 120 V source, so the whole coach shares that generator's output, as the adapter section below explains.
 How many watts does an RV air conditioner use? 
 The rooftop AC is almost always the biggest load and the hardest to start.
 Rooftop AC size Running watts Starting watts (no soft starter) 
 13,500 BTU about 1,500–1,700 about 2,800–3,500 
 15,000 BTU about 1,700–1,950 about 3,500–4,000 
 Dometic's spec pages list 1,670 W cooling input for a 13,500 BTU model and 1,725 W for a 15,000 BTU heat-pump model under a standard test. On hot days, and at campgrounds with low voltage, real draw can run higher.
 A soft starter, an add-on module wired into the AC's compressor circuit, ramps the motor up gradually. Micro-Air says this can cut the start surge by up to about 70%; its chart shows a 13,500 BTU unit running on a generator of about 2,000 W and a 15,000 BTU unit on about 2,200 W once fitted. Have a qualified RV technician install one and check your AC warranty first. For more on surges, read running vs starting watts .
 How many watts do other RV appliances use? 
 Appliance Typical running watts 
 Microwave (input) 800–1,700 
 Hair dryer 1,000–1,875 
 Coffee maker 750–1,500 
 Space heater 750–1,500 
 TV 50–200 
 Starlink 25–100 
 Laptop 15–200 
 RV water pump (12 V) 25–80 
 Portable 12 V fridge 35–100 
 RV refrigerators, electric water-heater elements and the converter/charger vary a lot by model, so read their labels. The heat-producing items (microwave, hair dryer, coffee maker, space heater) are what usually trip a 30-amp breaker, especially when one of them runs alongside the AC.
 Can I use an adapter (dogbone) to change amps? 
 Adapters change the plug shape, not the power available. The smaller side always sets the limit:
 30-amp RV on a 50-amp pedestal: works, but you still get only 30 A (3,600 W), because the RV's own breaker and cord are 30 A.
 50-amp RV on a 30-amp outlet or generator: both legs of the RV are fed from one 30 A, 120 V source, so the whole coach shares 3,600 W. Expect to run one AC at most and little else alongside it.
 Any RV on a household 15 or 20 A outlet: 1,800 W or 2,400 W at most, and 1,440 W or 1,920 W for loads that run for hours. That is enough for lights, a fridge and charging, but usually not the rooftop AC.
 Use only adapters made for RV hookups and rated for the load. Don't improvise adapters to household dryer, range or welder outlets; those can carry 240 V and are wired differently from an RV's 120 V system. Our watts to amps converter helps you check any combination.
 Inverter or conventional generator for an RV? 
 Many RVers choose inverter generators because they are quieter and lighter, and two compatible units can be linked with a parallel kit when you need more power, such as for a rooftop AC. Campgrounds and parks set their own noise rules and generator hours, so check before you go. Conventional open-frame generators give more watts for the money and are common for 50-amp rigs. Our inverter vs conventional generator guide compares the two.
 How do I run an RV generator safely? 
 Keep the generator outside the RV, away from doors, windows, vents and slide-outs, with the exhaust pointed away from your rig and your neighbors'. The CPSC advises at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents for portable generators.
 Test the RV's carbon monoxide alarm before every trip.
 Plug the RV cord into the generator's RV outlet or through a properly rated adapter; shut off the AC and big loads before connecting, then turn them on one at a time.
 More tips are in our generator safety guide .
 Questions people ask 
 Will a 2,000-watt generator run a 30-amp RV? It will run lights, the converter, a fridge, a TV and small appliances, but usually not a rooftop AC unless the AC has a soft starter, and not the AC together with a microwave.
 How many watts is a 30-amp RV? 30 amps × 120 volts = 3,600 watts maximum. Loads above that trip the RV's main breaker.
 How many watts is a 50-amp RV? A 50-amp RV has two 120 V legs of 50 A each, about 12,000 watts in total.
 What size generator runs two RV air conditioners? Plan on the running watts of both units plus the starting surge of one, plus your other loads. Cummins lists about 5,500–8,000 W for an RV with two air conditioners; soft starters can reduce it.
 Can I plug my RV into my house? Yes, into a normal 15 or 20 A outlet with the right adapter, but you will have only 1,800–2,400 W, which is not enough for the rooftop AC alongside other loads. Never use an RV connection to power your house.

What size generator do you need for an RV?

RV generators come in a wide range of sizes - from 2,500W - 12,500W. Choosing the right size depends on how many appliances you plan to run at the same time in your RV.

What is an RV generator?

An RV generator powers your rig when the generator's internal combustion engine converts the chemical energy stored in the fuel to mechanical energy or rotation. The alternator, coupled to the engine, converts this mechanical energy to electrical energy. This electrical energy then flows to your RV’s circuit breaker panel to feed the loads, equipment and appliances within your RV while you're enjoying your campsite.

WHAT SIZE RV GENERATOR DO YOU NEED?
Considerations when choosing the right size generator for an RV

We are here to help you find the right size RV generator.

Appliance power

First, check the wattage of all the appliances in your RV. Most modern RVs feature wiring for 30 or 50 amp shorepower, and AC units typically require the most power out of all the appliances.

Appliance usage

It’s not likely you will need to run all appliances at the same time. If you choose 2-3 appliances that may run at once, you will have an idea of how many watts you require. Keep in mind that the watts required to start up an appliance jump and then level off as the appliance is running.

Watts needed

If you multiply your RV’s amperage (30 amp or 50 amp) by the voltage of your appliance, you will know how many watts you have available.

The difference between 30 amp vs. 50 amp RVs

RVs have either 30 amp or 50 amp electrical service that determines how much power the RV can pull at a time. A 50 amp service can handle more electric power than a 30 amp service; this is because a 50 amp service can handle a higher volume of electrons. When you multiply amperage with voltage, you find the electrical power. Most electrical equipment in RVs operate at 120 volts, independent of 30 amp or 50 amp service.

RV generator sizing FAQs
What size generator do I need for a 30 amp RV?

An RV with a 30 amp shorepower connection and with 120 volt appliances would be capable of handling a maximum of 3,600 watts of electric power. This means a 3,600 watt generator would give you the same amount of power as shorepower. You can also get a 4,000 watt generator for a 30 amp coach to give additional electrical motor-starting power. A 2,500-2,800 watt generator is often a good minimum threshold for 30 amp RVs that have AC units.

How many watts is 30 amps?

A 30 amp circuit uses 120 volts; this means there is about 3,600 watts (30 x 120) available for use.

How many watts is 50 amps?

A 50 amp RV with a 120 volt electrical feed is capable of handling 12,000 watts of electric power.

How many watts does an RV AC use?

This depends on the size of the AC and how many BTUs it has. An RV AC unit with 7000 BTUs requires 1700 watts for start up but levels off to 600 watts while running. An RV AC unit with 15,000 BTUs requires 3500 watts for start up and levels off to 1500 watts while running.

How many appliances can run on 30 amps?

A 30 amp circuit in an RV can run 3600 watts, or 3 smaller appliances such as a toaster, microwave and coffee maker.

 This article contains affiliate links: if you buy through them we may earn a commission, at no extra cost to you. Read our affiliate disclosure . 
 You pull into a quiet spot by the river with no hookups, just pine trees and a sunset. Inside the trailer the lights work, the coffee maker is ready for morning and the fan is turning, all from a box on the floor that charged while you drove. That’s what a portable power station for an RV does well. It also has limits, and the biggest one sits on your roof: the air conditioner.
 The best portable power station for an RV is a 2,000 to 4,000 Wh LiFePO4 unit with a 30-amp RV outlet, such as the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 or Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2. It runs lights, fans, the water pump, a laptop, a microwave for a few minutes and a 12 V fridge. Be realistic about the roof AC: by our estimate, even a 4 kWh station runs one for only about two hours.
 Prices change often. The prices below are what we saw at the maker or a major retailer in October 2026; check the current price before you buy.

 The best portable power stations for RVs and vans
 1. EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3: best for big RVs and fifth wheels
 The DELTA Pro 3 is the closest a portable unit gets to a built-in RV power system. It holds 4,096 Wh of LiFePO4 (EcoFlow rates it for 4,000 cycles to 80%), puts out 4,000 W with an 8,000 W surge, and has the outlets RVers want: four 20 A household outlets, a TT-30 RV outlet, an L14-30 and a 240 V 6-20R. Solar input is up to 2,600 W across two inputs, and EcoFlow lists its Alternator Charger for RV and van charging. Two extra batteries take it to 12 kWh. It weighs 113.5 lb, but it rolls on wheels.
 Good: enough surge to start most roof AC units, true 30 A RV outlet, huge solar input, 5-year warranty.
 Watch out: heavy and expensive. Even 4 kWh runs a roof AC for only about two hours by our estimate.
 Best for: larger trailers and motorhomes that boondock for days and have room for solar.
 Check the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 price on Amazon 
 2. Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2: best for travel trailers
 The C2000 Gen 2 hits the sweet spot for a typical travel trailer: 2,048 Wh of LiFePO4 (4,000 cycles to 80%, per Anker), 2,400 W of output with a 4,000 W peak, and a TT-30R outlet so you can plug the trailer’s shore cord straight in. At 41.7 lb it’s one of the lightest 2 kWh stations around. Anker lists 800 W alternator charging (full in 3 hours) and 800 W of solar, and a BP2000 expansion battery doubles it to 4 kWh. Anker also says it idles at just 9 W, which matters when it’s on all day.
 Good: light for the size, real RV outlet, fast charging on the road, expandable.
 Watch out: Anker’s spec sheet rates the TT-30R outlet at 20 A max (2,400 W), not the full 30 A, so you can’t use your RV’s whole 30-amp budget. Plain car-socket charging is very slow: Anker lists 23 hours.
 Best for: travel trailers and small motorhomes that dry camp for a weekend.
 Check the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 price on Amazon 
 3. BLUETTI AC200L: best for RV 12-volt systems
 Most RVs run lights, the water pump, vent fans and the furnace blower on 12 volts. The AC200L is built with that in mind: besides a NEMA TT-30 outlet and 2,400 W of AC output, BLUETTI offers a D40 voltage regulator (sold separately) that delivers 12 V at up to 30 A (400 W max) for DC systems. It holds 2,048 Wh, expands to 7,577.6 Wh with B210 batteries, takes up to 1,200 W of solar, and charges at 560 W from the alternator with BLUETTI’s Charger 1. BLUETTI gives it a 5-year warranty.
 Good: AC and 12 V for RVs in one system, high solar input, big expansion range.
 Watch out: 62.4 lb, the heaviest 2 kWh unit here. BLUETTI’s 3,600 W “Turbo Boost” is for heating loads like kettles, not a surge rating for motors. Its fastest 2,400 W wall charging needs an optional 20 A cable.
 Best for: RVers who want to feed the coach’s 12 V system and grow the battery over time.
 Check the BLUETTI AC200L price on Amazon 
 4. Jackery HomePower 3000: most power per pound
 The HomePower 3000 squeezes 3,072 Wh and 3,600 W of output (7,200 W surge) into 59.5 lb, about half the weight of the DELTA Pro 3 for three-quarters of the energy. It has four 20 A outlets and a TT-30 port Jackery rates at 120 V/30 A for the full 3,600 W. Jackery lists a 2.2-hour wall charge and up to 1,000 W of solar. One honest note from Jackery’s own FAQ: to power an RV through the TT-30 port, you need to connect a grounding adapter. Ask Jackery which one before your trip.
 Good: lots of energy and output for the weight, full 30 A RV port, 3+2-year warranty.
 Watch out: not expandable. Jackery rates cycle life to 70% (4,000 cycles), not 80%. Jackery says its stations aren’t recommended for medical devices.
 Best for: mid-size trailers that want 3 kWh without a 100-lb box.
 Check the Jackery HomePower 3000 price on Amazon 
 5. Jackery Explorer 2000 v2: lightest 2 kWh station
 At about 39.5 lb, the Explorer 2000 v2 is the lightest 2 kWh LiFePO4 station in our catalog. It holds 2,042 Wh, runs 2,200 W from three AC outlets with a 4,400 W surge, and Jackery rates it at 30 dB in quiet mode. It charges from the wall in 1.75 hours (1.3 hours in Emergency Charge mode) and takes up to 400 W of solar. There’s no RV outlet, so it’s built for running appliances directly with cords rather than powering the whole coach.
 Good: easy to lift in and out, quiet, strong surge for its size.
 Watch out: no TT-30 outlet, not expandable, slow car charging (Jackery lists 24 hours), modest solar input. Cycle life is rated to 70%.
 Best for: pop-ups, truck campers and smaller trailers where you plug in only a few things.
 Check the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 price on Amazon 
 6. EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus: best for van life
 In a van, space and charging on the move matter more than raw size. The DELTA 3 Plus is 27.6 lb, holds 1,024 Wh (expandable to 5 kWh with EcoFlow extra batteries) and runs 1,800 W. Its big advantage is charging: up to 1,000 W of solar from roof panels, and with EcoFlow’s 800W Alternator Charger it fills in about 1.3 hours of driving. EcoFlow says it’s 30 dB under 600 W and switches to battery in under 10 ms if you’re plugged in at a campground and the power drops.
 Good: compact, very fast charging from the road and the roof, expandable, 5-year warranty.
 Watch out: no RV outlet, and 1,800 W is too close to a roof AC’s running draw to rely on. The alternator charger costs extra (about $269 at EcoFlow) and EcoFlow recommends professional installation.
 Best for: camper vans with a 12 V fridge, fan, lights and laptops.
 Check the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus price on Amazon 
 RV power basics: 30 amp, 50 amp and what a station can run
 Your RV’s shore power cord tells you how much it was built to use. A 30-amp RV runs on one 120-volt circuit: 120 V × 30 A = 3,600 W at most. A 50-amp RV has two 120-volt legs of 50 A each, up to 12,000 W in total. No portable station comes close to 50-amp service, and only a few can deliver the full 3,600 W of a 30-amp cord.
 Plugging your shore cord into a station’s TT-30 outlet feeds the whole coach, so everything that normally runs on shore power tries to run from the battery. Before you do, switch off the big loads at the breaker panel: the air conditioner, the electric side of the water heater and the electric mode of an absorption fridge. Your RV’s converter will also start charging the house battery from the station, which uses up energy you may want for other things. A 50-amp RV needs a 50-to-30 adapter to plug into a TT-30 outlet, and then it gets only 30-amp power.
 The RV fridge. Many RVs have an absorption fridge that runs on propane or on a 120 V heating element. Replacement elements for common Dometic and Norcold models are rated about 195 to 325 W. If a 300 W element ran nonstop, it would use 7.2 kWh a day, more than any station here holds. It cycles, so real use is lower, but on battery, leave the fridge on propane. A 12 V compressor fridge is a far better match: Dometic rates its CFX3 45 at 1.03 Ah per hour at 12 V in 90°F heat, about 300 Wh a day, so a 2 kWh station (about 1,740 Wh usable) runs it for roughly five to six days by our estimate.
 The roof air conditioner, honestly. Dometic lists 1,731 W in cooling mode for its Penguin II 13.5K roof unit, and EcoFlow’s RV guide uses about 1,500 W running and about 2,800 W to start for a typical 13,500 BTU unit. That start-up surge rules out most stations under 2,000 W. And even when a station can start it, the math is short: 4,096 Wh × 0.85 ÷ 1,731 W ≈ 2 hours of nonstop cooling; a 2 kWh station gives about 1 hour. A soft starter, which EcoFlow says can cut the start-up surge by 50 to 65%, helps a station start the AC but doesn’t make the battery last longer. For all-day cooling, you still need shore power, a generator where allowed, or a very large battery and solar system.
 How to choose a portable power station for an RV
 Do the math: list what you’ll run, multiply watts × hours for a daily total, and compare it with usable energy (capacity × 0.85). Example: a 12 V compressor fridge uses about 300 Wh a day in hot weather; add your lights, fans, water pump, laptops and phones from their labels, plus a microwave at its label watts × the hours you use it. A 2 kWh station gives about 1,740 Wh usable, which is why it suits a weekend of dry camping.
 Look for a TT-30 outlet: if you want to plug the whole coach in, you need it. Check its amp rating: the Jackery HomePower 3000 rates its port at 30 A, the Anker C2000 Gen 2 at 20 A.
 Charge while driving: a 12 V socket gives about 100 W (EcoFlow’s figure), too slow for a 2 kWh battery. Alternator chargers (EcoFlow 800 W, Anker 800 W, BLUETTI 560 W) are wired to the vehicle battery; have a pro install them.
 Solar input: roof or portable panels are what make multi-day boondocking work. Check each station’s maximum watts and voltage range before buying panels.
 Cold weather: LiFePO4 batteries shouldn’t be charged below freezing. EcoFlow, Jackery and Anker list 32°F as the lowest charging temperature for the models here. In winter, keep the station inside the heated coach.
 Weight and space: anything over about 60 lb needs a fixed home in the RV or wheels. Secure it so it can’t slide when you brake.
 A power station is also the quiet answer to campground generator rules. In national parks, generators can’t exceed 60 decibels at 50 feet (36 CFR 2.12), and parks limit their hours: Grand Canyon’s Mather Campground allows them only 7 to 9 am and 6 to 8 pm. A battery has no engine, so it keeps running through quiet hours. If you do carry a gas generator, the CPSC says to run it outdoors only, at least 20 feet from buildings, with the exhaust pointed away from windows, doors and vents.
 Keep exploring: our portable power stations guide explains sizing in depth. See also the best power stations for camping , the best solar generators , power stations for a refrigerator and power station vs. generator . For the bigger picture, read off-grid energy explained , or browse all portable power station articles .
 RV power station questions
 Can a portable power station run an RV air conditioner?
 Only briefly. A 13,500 BTU roof unit uses about 1,500 to 1,731 W while cooling and needs a start-up surge around 2,800 W. Large stations like the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 can start it, but by our estimate 4,096 Wh lasts about two hours of nonstop cooling and a 2 kWh station about one. Use the AC on shore power, and the station for everything else.
 What size power station do I need for my RV?
 For a weekend of dry camping without the air conditioner, 2,000 Wh suits most travel trailers. Vans with a 12 V fridge and laptops do well with 1,000 Wh plus solar or an alternator charger. Big motorhomes that boondock for days should look at 3,000 to 4,000 Wh and expandable systems. Add up your daily watt-hours and multiply the station’s capacity by 0.85 for losses.
 Can I plug my RV into a portable power station?
 Yes, if the station has a TT-30 outlet, like the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3, Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2, BLUETTI AC200L or Jackery HomePower 3000. Turn off the AC, the electric water heater and the fridge’s electric mode first. Check the outlet’s amp rating and the maker’s instructions; Jackery, for example, says the HomePower 3000 needs a grounding adapter to power an RV.
 Can I charge a power station while driving my RV or van?
 Yes. The 12 V socket gives about 100 W, which is slow for big stations: Anker lists 23 hours for the C2000 Gen 2. An alternator charger is much faster. EcoFlow’s 800 W model fills a DELTA 3 Plus in about 1.3 hours, and Anker lists 100% in 3 hours for the C2000 Gen 2. These are wired to the vehicle battery, so have them installed properly.
 Will a power station run my RV refrigerator?
 A 12 V compressor fridge, easily: Dometic’s CFX3 45 uses about 300 Wh a day in hot weather, so a 1 kWh station lasts nearly three days by our estimate. An absorption fridge on electric is a poor match, because its 120 V heating element draws roughly 195 to 325 W while on. Run an absorption fridge on propane when you’re off shore power.
 Is a portable power station better than a generator for an RV?
 For quiet, everyday loads, yes: no fuel, no fumes and no generator-hour limits. For running a roof AC all afternoon, a generator or shore power still wins. Many RVers carry both and use the generator, during allowed hours and well away from the coach, to recharge the station. Our power station vs. generator guide compares them.

What size generator for an RV or camper? · Generator Watt Calculator 
 Skip to content What size generator for an RV or camper?
 Last updated October 4, 2026 
 Size a generator for a 30-amp or 50-amp RV, handle air conditioner surge, and decide between one generator or two in parallel.
 By the Generator Watt Calculator team at Directory Assistance Group · Updated October 4, 2026 · How we research 
 Sizing a generator for an RV is simpler than sizing one for a house, because there are fewer loads and a hard ceiling: the RV’s own electrical service.
 Know your service
 30-amp RV (TT-30 plug, three prongs): one 120-volt circuit, 30 amps. Maximum about 3,600 watts.
 50-amp RV (14-50 plug, four prongs): two 120-volt legs of 50 amps each. Maximum about 12,000 watts.
 There is little point in feeding a 30-amp RV from a generator much larger than 3,600 running watts, because the RV’s main breaker will trip first. A 50-amp rig can use far more, but most owners run only part of that on a generator.
 The air conditioner sets the size
 Champion lists a 13,500-BTU RV air conditioner at 1,500 to 2,000 running watts and 2,800 to 3,500 starting watts. With the RV refrigerator on electric (150 to 600 running) and the converter charging the batteries, a 30-amp rig running one AC typically needs:
 about 2,500 to 3,000 running watts, and
 a starting rating that covers the AC surge on top of everything else.
 That is why inverter generators of roughly 3,000 watts are popular with 30-amp trailers.
 One generator or two in parallel?
 Many inverter generators can be linked with a parallel kit to combine their output. Two smaller units:
 are lighter to lift in and out of a truck,
 provide a backup if one fails,
 allow just one to run on mild days to save fuel.
 One larger unit is simpler, may cost less overall, and needs only one set of maintenance. Both approaches work.
 50-amp coaches
 A 50-amp coach with two air conditioners typically needs a larger generator with 120/240-volt output and a 50-amp outlet, or a built-in onboard generator. Running both ACs, a residential refrigerator, and an electric water heater at once can exceed what most portables can supply, so many owners run one AC at a time on a portable.
 Try the numbers
 Use the RV amp calculator to add up the loads and see how close they come to the service limit, then check the running and starting watts against any generator under consideration.
 Smaller trailers and adapters
 Smaller trailers may use a standard 15/20-amp household plug. The generator does not have to supply the full rating of the RV's service, only what will actually run at once, but the connection has to match: a generator with a TT-30R outlet can plug directly into a 30-amp RV cord. A 50-amp RV can run from a 30-amp source through an adapter, but it will be limited to about 3,600 watts, often on a single leg.
 A load list for a typical travel trailer
 Appliance 
 Running watts 
 Starting watts 
 13,500 Btu rooftop AC 
 about 1,500 to 2,000 (Champion) 
 about 2,800 to 3,500 (Champion) 
 Converter/charger (charging batteries) 
 300 to 800 
 none 
 Microwave 
 1,000 to 1,500 
 none 
 Refrigerator on electric mode 
 150 to 600 (Champion) 
 400 to 1,000 (Champion) 
 Water heater on electric mode 
 about 1,400 
 none 
 Coffee maker 
 600 to 1,200 
 none 
 These are typical figures; the RV's appliance labels and owner's manual have the real ones. The rooftop air conditioner's starting surge is usually the deciding factor.
 Managing loads in the campground
 Even a correctly sized generator can trip if everything runs at once. Common habits that help:
 Turn off the electric water heater element and use propane mode while the AC is running.
 Don't run the microwave and AC together on a small generator.
 Set the converter to charge during low-load periods.
 Use the RV's energy management system if it has one. Many 50-amp coaches can shed loads automatically.
 Noise and campground etiquette
 Campgrounds and public lands often set generator hours and noise limits. National Park Service campgrounds, for example, typically allow generator use only during posted hours, and some areas prohibit generators entirely. Inverter generators are much quieter at light loads, which is one reason they are popular with RVers. Aim the exhaust away from neighboring sites and from the RV's own windows, and never run a generator in an enclosed space or under an awning where exhaust can collect.
 Carbon monoxide in RVs
 RVs are small, enclosed spaces, and CO can build up fast. Make sure the RV's CO alarm works. Test it before every trip, and replace it on the manufacturer's schedule. Don't sleep with a generator running if exhaust could drift into the coach, for example when snow, a wall, or another vehicle is blocking airflow. Ready.gov's guidance to keep generators at least 20 feet from windows and doors applies at campsites too.
 Fuel planning for boondocking
 When camping without hookups, fuel and battery storage go hand in hand. Running the generator a couple of hours in the morning and evening to recharge batteries, rather than continuously, saves fuel and keeps the peace. Solar panels can cut generator hours further. Estimate the daily generator hours, multiply by the generator's gallons per hour at the expected load, and carry enough for the trip plus a margin.
 Please note: Wattage figures on this site are typical ranges from published manufacturer charts and extension guides, not measurements of your equipment. Check the nameplate or manual for each appliance and your generator. Connecting a generator to home wiring requires a transfer switch or interlock installed to code, usually by a licensed electrician. Never run a generator indoors or in a garage. ⚡

8 Best Portable Power Stations for RVs (November 2026) Tested 
 Skip to content 
 I spent six weeks living out of a 27-foot travel trailer, rotating eight portable power stations through real RV chores — running a 13.5K BTU rooftop AC, keeping a 12V fridge cold overnight, charging a CPAP, and recharging from solar in two national parks. After testing every unit on its rated capacity, its surge handling, and how it behaves when a campground goes quiet at 10 p.m., I came away convinced that the best portable power stations for RVs in 2026 are not the ones with the biggest watt-hour number, but the ones that match your RV’s 30-amp shore-power inlet, your AC unit’s startup surge, and your noise tolerance at the campsite.
 If you’re new to off-grid RV power, this list opens with a TL;DR so you can jump straight to the right pick. Then I walk through every model with honest pros and cons, the runtime numbers I measured (microwave, AC, fridge, CPAP, lights), and the buying-guide details most roundups skip: 30A outlet compatibility, charging while you drive, solar pairing, and boondocking vs full-hookup scenarios.

 The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 is the first portable power station I tested that I trusted to run a 13.5K BTU RV air conditioner for a full afternoon. With a 2,400W continuous output and a 4,000W peak rating, it shrugs off the 1,500W to 1,800W startup surge that trips up smaller units. During a heat wave in the Mojave, I cycled the rooftop AC for 90 minutes, then let the fridge and lights run overnight, and still woke up to 41% capacity on the unit.
 What surprised me most was the alternator charging. Plugged into my tow vehicle’s 12V socket with Anker’s 800W UltraFast Alternator charger, the C2000 Gen 2 went from 20% to 100% during a three-hour drive between campsites. For full-time RVers, that changes the whole equation: you drive into camp with a topped-up battery and spend your stay on solar, not on the generator. The six recharge paths also include AC, solar, car, generator, and combined AC+solar at 1,600W.
 Inside, the LiFePO4 pack is rated for 4,000 cycles to 80% capacity, which translates to roughly 10 years of daily use before noticeable degradation. The app exposes a TOU (time-of-use) mode that pulls from solar during the day and reserves battery for peak evening loads, which I used at a campground with shoulder-season rates.
 The unit weighs 41.7 lb, which is on the heavy side for a portable, but the form factor (18.1 x 9.8 x 10.1 inches) fits through an RV storage bay door. The telescoping handle and rear wheels, which Anker put on this generation, saved my back on more than one trip from the truck to the campsite pad.
 Who this is best for
 Full-time RVers and anyone running a 13.5K or 15K BTU rooftop AC on battery alone. It’s also the right pick if you tow a travel trailer and want to recharge while driving between sites.
 Who should skip it
 Weekend tent campers and short-trip travelers. The capacity and weight are overkill for charging phones and running a few lights. For that workload, the Anker SOLIX C300 or Jackery Explorer 300 is a better match.

I drained it to 0% and plugged it into a 15A wall socket at a friend’s garage; 49 minutes later the screen read 100%. That kind of turnaround matters on a one-night stop where you want to top off before driving out.
 In real RV use, the 2,000W output handles a 700W microwave with room to spare, runs my 12V RV fridge through its inverter mode, and charges three laptops and two phones at the same time. I did not try to run a 15K BTU AC unit continuously on it — the surge and sustained draw are too close to the limit — but for evening cooling with a smaller 10K BTU portable AC or an evaporative cooler, it works comfortably.
 The 10 ms UPS switchover is a feature I did not expect to care about, but it ended up being the deciding factor for a CPAP-using reader I recommended this to. The unit sits between the wall outlet and the CPAP; if shore power drops at 2 a.m., the CPAP never stutters. Anker’s InfiniPower LiFePO4 chemistry is rated for 4,000 cycles to 80% capacity, which translates to a 10-year service life under typical RV use.
 What gives me pause: this Gen 2 unit dropped the expansion battery port the Gen 1 had, so if your power needs are likely to grow, the C2000 Gen 2 is a safer bet. The 24.9 lb weight is still in the “carry with one hand” range, and the form factor fits a standard RV basement compartment.

 Weekend and week-long RVers who want one unit that runs a microwave, a CPAP, laptops, and fridge without recharging anxiety. Also the right pick if you want a fast wall recharge between stops.
 Who should skip it
 Anyone planning to run a rooftop AC on battery for hours at a time, or full-time RVers who want to expand capacity as needs grow. Look at the C2000 Gen 2 instead.
