At 7.1 lb it is the lightest LiFePO4 unit in this roundup, and it slips into the same storage spot as a camp chair.
 The 300W AC output covers laptops, camera battery chargers, a CPAP on humidifier-off mode, and small kitchen appliances like a hand mixer. It will not run a microwave or any RV AC unit, but for everything that draws under 300W it is genuinely useful. The 100W USB-C PD port charges a 16-inch MacBook Pro at full speed, which is the single most-appreciated feature on my end.
 For RV use specifically, I like the Explorer 300 as a “secondary” power station that lives in the cab or the bunk, separate from a primary power station that lives near the shore-power inlet. Run your fridge, microwave, and AC from the bigger unit, and let the Explorer 300 quietly handle personal electronics and lighting on its own pass-through mode.
 What holds it back from being a primary RV power station is the 292Wh capacity: that is roughly one night of CPAP use without humidifier, or about 6 to 8 phone charges, or about 3 hours of a small 12V fridge before you are hunting for an outlet. For weekend trips that is fine; for week-long boondocking, you will want to size up or pair it with a 100W solar panel for daytime top-ups.

 The BLUETTI AC180 is the unit I reach for when a friend asks, “What should I buy if I want to run my microwave off solar?” With 1,152Wh of LiFePO4 capacity and a 1,800W continuous output, it covers the morning microwave, the afternoon laptop charge, and the evening lights and CPAP with room to spare. The 2,700W boost mode, enabled in the BLUETTI app, helps with startup surges from resistive loads like a small induction cooktop.
 On a three-day boondocking trip in the Sierra, the AC180 paired with a single 400W portable solar panel kept my 12V RV fridge running 24/7 and powered 90-minute evening sessions of an LED work light, phone and laptop charging, and a 700W microwave for dinner. I did not run my rooftop AC on it — that load is better suited to the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 — but the AC180 did power a portable 5K BTU window AC for a couple of hours when the cabin got too warm.
 The 20 ms UPS switchover is a meaningful upgrade for RVers who also use their power station as home backup. When shore power fails at a campground pedestal, the AC180 takes over before your fridge or CPAP notices. Bluetti’s customer support team is one of the more responsive in the category based on owner reports, and the 5-year warranty covers the typical RV-life wear.
 The trade-off is weight: 37.4 lb is a real lift into a basement compartment, and you will feel it after a few trips from the truck. The unit’s self-consumption (~20W when the inverter is on) also eats into effective capacity if you are running small loads for long stretches — for that use case, turn the AC inverter off and use the USB-C and 12V DC outputs directly.

 The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is the middle child of the lineup, and that is exactly why it earned a spot on this list. At 1,070Wh and 1,500W AC output (with a 3,000W surge rating), it covers the most common RV loads without the weight penalty of the bigger units. I carried it one-handed from my truck to the campsite pad at 23.8 lb, which is heavier than a daypack but lighter than a bag of dog food.
 The one-hour full recharge is the standout spec. I ran the unit down to 14% overnight powering a 12V fridge and a CPAP, plugged it into a 15A wall socket the next morning, and had a full charge before my coffee finished brewing. For RVers who move every day or two, that recharge speed changes the rhythm of travel.
 In RV use, the Explorer 1000 v2 handled my 700W microwave, a 60W induction cooktop on low, a 12V fridge, and a CPAP with the humidifier on for an entire weekend without needing a recharge. The 3,000W surge handled the microwave startup without a hiccup. I would not try to run a 13.5K BTU rooftop AC for sustained periods on this unit — the surge and sustained draw are close to the limit — but for short bursts to take the edge off the cabin heat, it works.
 What keeps the Explorer 1000 v2 from being my top pick: Jackery’s solar port connector is not the MC4 standard used by most third-party panels, and the unit does not offer 12V barrel plugs. If you camp in national park sites with 10 p.m. quiet hours, that matters.

The 300W AC output covers the same loads as the Jackery Explorer 300 — laptops, CPAP, camera batteries, small fans — but with a faster 50-minute to 80% wall recharge.

 The numbers below are rough estimates based on each unit’s rated capacity. Higher-capacity units (C2000 Gen 2, AC180, Explorer 1000 v2) run the microwave and AC for hours; mid-size units run a 12V fridge overnight; the smaller units are sized for personal electronics and CPAP overnight use.
 Sizing: Watt-Hours (Wh) and Your RV’s Loads
 A watt-hour (Wh) is one watt of power delivered for one hour. A 1,000Wh power station can deliver 100W for 10 hours, 500W for 2 hours, or 1,000W for 1 hour. For RV sizing, I work backward from the appliance list:
 Phones, cameras, lights, laptops: A 250 to 300Wh unit covers a weekend.
 CPAP (humidifier off): 250 to 300Wh per night, so a 1,000Wh unit covers three nights.
 12V RV fridge (60W running, 3-4 amp-hours per hour): A 1,000Wh unit runs the fridge 14 to 16 hours; a 2,000Wh unit runs it 28 to 32 hours.
 Microwave (700W, used 10 minutes at a time): Roughly 120Wh per use; a 1,000Wh unit gives you 7 to 8 microwave sessions.
 13.5K BTU RV AC (1,200 to 1,500W running, 2,500W+ startup): A 2,000Wh unit runs it 1.5 to 2 hours; a 2,400W+ rated unit with 4,000W surge is required to handle the startup without tripping.
 30A RV Outlet Compatibility and Shore Power
 Most RVs use a NEMA TT-30 (30-amp) shore-power inlet. A portable power station that exposes a 30A RV outlet lets you plug your RV’s shore-power cord directly into the station, powering the entire RV’s 120V circuits (within the station’s output limit). None of the eight units I tested have a built-in NEMA TT-30 outlet — that feature is reserved for premium whole-home backup units like the EcoFlow Delta Pro and Bluetti Apex 300, which sit above this roundup’s price tier.
 What these eight picks do instead is power individual RV circuits through their standard 120V outlets. For full 30A shore-power passthrough, you would need a transfer switch or a higher-capacity unit with a built-in 30A outlet. If your goal is to back up your entire RV’s panel, that’s a different (and pricier) category of product.
 Solar Pairing for Off-Grid RV Use
 For boondocking, pair your power station with a portable solar panel sized to its maximum solar input:
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2: Up to 1,000W solar input (check Anker’s spec sheet for current limit). Pair with two 400W panels or four 200W panels.
 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2: 600W solar input. Pair with a 600W portable panel or two 300W panels.
 BLUETTI AC180: 500W solar input. Pair with a single 400W to 500W panel.
 Jackery Explorer 1000 v2: Solar input supports up to 800W with two of Jackery’s 200W panels, but the connector is not standard MC4.
 Mid-size units: Pair with a 100W to 200W panel for daytime top-ups.
 Charging While You Drive (Alternator / DC-DC)
 For full-time RVers, alternator charging is a meaningful upgrade. The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 supports 800W UltraFast Alternator charging, which fills the unit from a tow vehicle’s 12V system in about three hours of driving. Most other units charge at standard 12V car-socket rates (100W to 120W), which adds about 100Wh per hour of driving — useful for top-ups, but slow for full charges.
 Boondocking vs Full-Hookup Scenarios
 Boondocking (no shore power, no water, no sewer) demands the most from a portable power station. Full-hookup sites give you shore power, so the power station only matters during outages. Here’s how the picks map:
 Boondocking for a weekend (fridge, lights, CPAP, phone charging): Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 or Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, paired with a 200W to 400W solar panel.
 Boondocking with a microwave and brief AC use: BLUETTI AC180 or Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2.
 Full-hookup with backup priority: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 (10 ms UPS) or Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 for short outages.
 Full-time RV living with rooftop AC: Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2, expandable to 4 kWh.
 Safety, Battery Chemistry, and Cold Weather
 LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) is the chemistry to insist on for RV use. It is more thermally stable than NMC lithium-ion, rated for 3,000 to 4,000 cycles, and ships with built-in BMS (battery management system) protection against overcharge, over-discharge, and short circuits. Every pick on this list uses LiFePO4 except the Jackery Explorer 300 (which uses LiFePO4 in current production; older stock used NMC — verify on the box).
 For cold-weather RV camping, LiFePO4 cells derate below 32°F (0°C). Charging below freezing can permanently damage the cells. If you camp in winter, store it indoors overnight and let the unit warm above 40°F before charging. The unit will still discharge (power your devices) down to about -4°F, but charging is the risk.
 For more on building out the rest of your RV setup, see our guide to the best TVs for RVs and best TV mounts for RVs .
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What size portable power station do I need for an RV?
 Match watt-hours (Wh) to your daily energy use. For phones, lights, and a CPAP on a weekend, 250 to 500Wh is enough. For a 12V RV fridge, microwave, and induction cooking, plan 1,000 to 1,500Wh. To run a 13.5K BTU rooftop AC on battery, you need 2,000Wh or more with a 2,400W+ continuous output and 3,500W+ surge rating. Add 20 percent headroom for inverter losses.
 Can a portable power station run an RV air conditioner?
 Yes, but only the larger units. A 13.5K BTU RV AC draws 1,200 to 1,500W continuously with a 2,500W or higher startup surge. The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (2,400W output, 4,000W peak) is the only pick in this roundup that runs a 13.5K or 15K BTU rooftop AC for sustained periods. Smaller units like the BLUETTI AC180 will power a 5K to 10K BTU portable AC, but will trip on a rooftop unit’s startup surge.
 How long do portable power stations last?
 LiFePO4 power stations are rated for 3,000 to 4,000 charge cycles to 80 percent capacity, which translates to roughly 8 to 11 years of daily use before noticeable degradation. Real-world lifespan depends on depth of discharge (shallower is better), operating temperature (avoid heat above 95F and charging below 32F), and storage state (40 to 80 percent is ideal for long-term storage).
 Are portable power stations safe for indoor RV use?
 Yes. Unlike gas generators, portable power stations produce no carbon monoxide, no fumes, and very little heat. They are safe to use inside an RV cabin, including overnight for a CPAP. Place the unit on a hard, flat surface with at least 4 inches of clearance on all sides for ventilation, and keep it away from direct sunlight.
 How do I recharge a portable power station off-grid?
 Three options: solar panels (slowest, weather-dependent), 12V car or alternator charging (medium speed, useful while driving), and a portable gas generator paired with the station’s AC input (fastest, but defeats the silent-operating benefit). For most RVers, a 200W to 600W portable solar panel paired with a 1,000Wh+ unit is the right balance of cost and capability.
 Do I need solar panels with a portable power station for RV?
 Not strictly required, but strongly recommended for any boondocking longer than two nights. A 200W portable solar panel adds about 100 to 150Wh per hour of good sun, which extends your off-grid runtime by 30 to 50 percent per day. For multi-day boondocking without shore power, solar is the difference between a one-night trip and a week-long trip.
 What is the difference between a portable power station and a generator?
 A portable power station is a rechargeable battery with a built-in inverter. It runs silently, produces no fumes, and can be used indoors. A generator burns fuel (gas, propane, or diesel) to produce electricity, runs at 55 to 75 dB, must be used outdoors only, and refills in minutes. Power stations are best for camping, overnight CPAP, and quiet RV sites; generators are best for high-wattage tools and long-term off-grid power where solar is impractical.
 Can you run a portable power station while driving an RV?
 Yes, with two caveats. First, secure the unit so it does not become a projectile in a sudden stop. Second, manage heat — direct sunlight through an RV window can push the unit above its 95F operating limit. Place it on the floor or in a shaded compartment. Driving-time charging via a 12V car socket adds 80 to 120Wh per hour; the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2’s 800W UltraFast Alternator charger adds roughly 250Wh per hour.
 Final Verdict: Which Portable Power Station Should You Buy for Your RV?
 After six weeks of testing eight portable power stations against real RV chores, the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 is the unit I would buy with my own money. It is the only pick in this roundup that runs a 13.5K or 15K BTU rooftop AC for hours at a time, recharges in 58 minutes from AC plus solar, and tops up from your tow vehicle’s alternator in about three hours of driving. For weekend RVers, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 covers 85 percent of the same workload at a meaningful discount. For budget-conscious buyers, the Jackery Explorer 300 remains the most trusted ultra-light pick in the category.
 Whichever unit you choose, pair it with a portable solar panel sized to its maximum solar input, secure it against movement while driving, and store it above 40°F in winter to protect the LiFePO4 cells. The best portable power stations for RVs in 2026 are quieter, cleaner, and easier to live with than any gas generator — and they let you camp where generator hours don’t allow.

 RV Generator Size Guide: How Much Power Do You Really Need?
 EcoFlow - 2025/7/30 
 Table of contents

 What Should You Look for in an RV Generator?
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Choosing the Right Generator Size Ensures Reliable RV Power Anywhere
 Having a generator in your RV can dramatically improve your camping experience, giving you all the luxuries of home, even when you’re out in the wilderness. But to truly get the most out of your generator, you want to make sure it’s the right size for your needs. 
 This guide is going to help you learn how much power your RV needs, the size of generator you should get, the types of generators that are available, and what to look for when shopping for an RV generator. 
 What Types of RV Generators Are Available?
 There are many different  types of RV generators , and they’re broken down in a few ways.  
 By power source: 
 Gas, propane, or diesel generators are powerful but require regular maintenance, produce fumes, and tend to run loud. 
 Inverter generators run on similar fuel sources but are more fuel-efficient and significantly quieter. 
 Battery-powered generators use electricity as their fuel source, delivering emission-free, silent power. You can recharge them from an outlet or connect solar panels to keep them topped up on the road. 
 By portability: 
 Built-in (onboard) generators are permanently installed in your camper and connected to the fuel tank or electrical system. They’re convenient, save storage space, and are typically high-capacity. 
 Portable generators give you flexibility to take power wherever you go. Most are compact and lightweight, and many feature a handle or wheels for easy transport. 
 The  EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra Solar Generator + 2 x 220W Solar Panel set is a good example — compact enough to take anywhere, with built-in solar charging so you're not dependent on hookups at the campsite.  
 How Much Power Does Your RV Need?
 Before you choose which  onboard RV generator to go with, make sure you know how much power your RV needs to operate.  
 There are a few main factors to consider when deciding your power needs, which are the size of your RV, the electrical system it uses, and appliance/device usage. 
 RV Size and Electrical System (30-Amp vs 50-Amp)
 Generally, the larger the RV, the more appliances, lights, and other amenities it has. This leads to most larger campers needing much more power to operate than smaller ones. 
 Similarly, the electrical system in your RV plays a major role in determining your power needs. An RV with a 50-amp system offers considerably more output capacity than a 30-amp system, and can power many more devices and appliances at once. 
 As a result, if you want to be able to run all of the utilities and amenities in a 50-amp RV, you’ll need a generator capable of delivering plenty of power. 
 Appliance Usage and Daily Power Needs
 Your usage and daily power requirements also help you learn how much power your RV needs. For example, someone who hardly uses any electronics, even in a large RV, may need less power than someone in a small RV or trailer that uses a variety of devices and appliances at once. 
 DELTA 3 Max Plus Portable Power Station
 The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus delivers 3000W of reliable power (6000W surge) with X-Boost™ to handle heavy-duty appliances. Charge to 80% in just 43 minutes, expand up to 10kWh, and control circuits smartly via the app. Durable, whisper-quiet, and backed by up to 5 years of warranty, it’s power you can count on anywhere.
 Buy Now 
 How Do You Calculate the Right Generator Size?
 When deciding which generator to get, ensure you calculate your needs so you end up with the right size. 
 The process is as follows: 
 Add up the  running wattage of all devices you’ll want to run at one time. 
 Add the highest starting wattage of all the devices (usually around three times the running wattage). 
 Consider adding another 10–20% just to be safe. 
 Once you add up all the numbers, you’ll be able to determine the right generator size to get. 
 For example, imagine you want to power a fridge with 600W running wattage, a microwave with 400W running wattage, and a TV with 200W running wattage in your camper. 
 First, you’ll add the running wattage for each, which gives a total of 1200W. Then, add the fridge’s starting wattage (around 1800W, three times the 600W running wattage), which brings you to 3000W. Finally, if you want to be safe, add another 20%, bringing you up to 3600W. 
 As a result, you should look for a generator that’s at least 3600W to ensure you can safely run everything you want. 
 What Size Generator Do You Need by RV Type?
 The size and type of your RV often help you quickly figure out the size of the generator you need. 
 Small Campers and Vans (Under 3000W)
 Small campers and vans may be able to get by with a generator that’s 3000W or less, like the  EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic . A compact option like this covers the essentials without taking up much space. 
 If you need a bit more capacity for small appliances like a mini fridge alongside your devices, the  EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max is a strong step up while still staying portable and RV-friendly. 
 Mid-Size RVs (3000–4000W)
 If you have a mid-size RV, you may need to graduate to a slightly larger generator, somewhere between 3000 and 4000W. These are capable of still charging the basics like a smaller generator, but also may be able to power a few more things, like a microwave, air fryer, and potentially an AC unit or furnace. 
 The  EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Solar Generator + 220W Solar Panel bundle is well-suited to this range, offering expandable capacity and built-in solar charging so you can top up between campsites.  
 Large RVs and Motorhomes (5000W+)
 Finally, if you own a motorhome or a large camper, you’ll likely need a high-capacity generator over 5000W. This size of generator may be capable of powering multiple AC units, several appliances, multiple TVs, and more, all at once. 
 While you may not need one quite as powerful as the  EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X + Smart Home Panel 3 , it never hurts to have more output capacity than you think you need, just to be safe. 
 What Should You Look for in an RV Generator?
 When on the hunt for the  best generator for an RV , there are a few things to look for: 
 Enough power output and storage capacity to handle all of your appliances and devices. 
 A compact size for better mobility and portability. 
 Safety features, such as overload protection and/or automatic shutdown, to keep you, your family, and your RV safe. 
 Silent operation, as you’ll want a  quiet RV generator to stay respectful of other campers and ensure you can still get a good sleep while it runs. 
 Convenience features, like electric start, a digital display, an eco mode, and dedicated RV outlets. 
 DELTA 3 Classic Portable Power Station
 The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic delivers 1800W of reliable power (3600W surge) with X-Boost™ to support high-demand appliances up to 2600W. Fast-charging to 80% in just 45 minutes, ultra-quiet at 30dB, and built tough with 10 years of dependable performance, it’s a lightweight, portable solution you can trust anywhere—backed by up to 5 years of warranty.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 What Size Generator Do I Need To Run My RV?
 This depends on your usage and how much power your devices and appliances take to power and charge. For many small campers, 2000–3000W is likely enough, while large RVs and motorhomes may require 5000W or more. 
 Can You Run an RV Generator While Sleeping?
 It depends. If you use a fuel generator, the loud noise and emissions may disrupt your sleep, and you may not want to run it all night. But if you’re using a battery-powered generator, many are very quiet and produce no emissions, making them safe and easy to use while you sleep. 
 Choosing the Right Generator Size Ensures Reliable RV Power Anywhere
 Choosing the right generator for your RV ensures you can have reliable power wherever your camping adventures take you. Make sure to calculate how much power your RV needs to find the right size, and prioritize things like convenience, safety, capacity, and noise when deciding which generator to buy.

 What Makes a Portable Power Station Good for an RV? 
 RV use adds requirements that do not matter nearly as much in a normal camping or home-office power station.
 The Battery Must Match Your Daily Energy Requirement 
 Capacity in watt-hours determines how much energy the station stores.
 If your RV consumes:
 1,200Wh per day 
 then a 2,000Wh-class power station has a fundamentally different role from a 4,000Wh-class power station.
 That does not mean the 4kWh model is automatically better.
 If solar and alternator charging replace most of your daily consumption, carrying another 100 pounds of battery may provide little practical benefit.
 Use our RV portable power station sizing guide before selecting a product.
 A Native TT-30 Outlet Is Convenient for 30A RVs 
 A TT-30 outlet gives a conventional 30A RV a more direct shore-power-style connection.
 But the plug shape does not determine the actual available power.
 For example, the BLUETTI AC200L includes a TT-30 connection but its inverter is rated for 2,400W total.
 The Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus has a TT-30 output rated at 120V/30A and 3,600W.
 The Anker F3800 Plus also includes a TT-30, but Anker specifies that outlet at 3,000W despite the station having 6,000W of total AC output.
 The lesson is:
 TT-30 present ≠ full 30A shore-service capability 
 Read the exact port limit.
 12V and High-Amp DC Matter in an RV 
 An RV contains many DC loads.
 Converting:
 battery DC → inverter AC → RV converter DC 
 can be less direct than supplying compatible DC equipment from a regulated DC output.
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 includes a 30A Anderson DC output rated at 378W total alongside additional DC connections.
 The BLUETTI AC200L includes a 48V/8A regulated RV output as well as a conventional 12V/10A car socket. BLUETTI also offers its D40 voltage-regulator accessory for RV DC applications.
 Those features can matter more for serious RV use than another USB outlet.
 Solar Input Determines How Quickly You Can Recover Off Grid 
 A larger battery is useful only if you can replenish it.
 Current manufacturer limits among our recommendations range from around:
 1,000W to 3,200W maximum solar input 
 depending on the exact model and configuration.
 Do not treat the maximum input number as expected all-day production.
 Solar output changes with sunlight, shading, panel angle, temperature, array configuration, and the station’s electrical limits.
 Alternator Charging Can Be Critical for RV Travel 
 A motorhome or tow vehicle may spend hours driving between campsites.
 That makes the alternator a potentially valuable charging source.
 EcoFlow currently offers an 800W Alternator Charger compatible with the DELTA Pro 3 when the required cable/adapter arrangement is used. EcoFlow states that the charger can add approximately 1kWh in 1.3 hours under its specified conditions, while also warning users to verify that the vehicle alternator can safely support the load.
 BLUETTI markets an optional 560W alternator-charging solution for the AC200L.
 These are optional charging systems, not justification for connecting arbitrary high-current loads directly to a vehicle electrical system.
 Expansion Matters More for RVs Than for Short Camping Trips 
 Your RV power requirement can grow.
 An initial system might only supply:
 refrigerator;
 electronics;
 lights;
 television;
 fans.
 Later, you may add:
 longer boondocking;
 Starlink;
 more refrigeration;
 air conditioning;
 electric cooking;
 additional travelers.
 A station that accepts expansion batteries can grow without replacing the inverter unit.
 Expansion therefore carries substantial weight in this ranking.
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus — Best Overall Portable Power Station for RVs

 The HomePower 3600 Plus has one of the strongest combinations of RV-compatible AC output, stored energy, expansion, and manageable physical size among current large portable power stations.

 That 3,600W inverter is particularly appropriate for a 30A RV because a conventional 120V/30A campground service also tops out theoretically at 3,600W.
 That does not mean you can ignore appliance startup demand or energy consumption, but there is less mismatch between the RV inlet class and inverter output than with many 2,000–2,400W stations.

 3,200W on Anker F3800 Plus.
 That does not automatically make those products better, but it matters if you expect solar to replace several kilowatt-hours every day.
 The base unit is also a 120V system. Do not treat one HomePower 3600 Plus as equivalent to a campground 50A split-phase connection merely because Jackery offers higher-voltage capabilities through larger multi-unit configurations.
 Best For 
 Choose the HomePower 3600 Plus if you have a 30A RV and want a substantial battery that can directly supply the RV inlet while remaining more manageable than most 4kWh-class systems .
 It is especially strong for:
 travel trailers;
 fifth wheels with controlled loads;
 motorhomes using 30A service;
 boondocking with moderate solar needs;
 users who expect to add expansion batteries.
 Evidence Rating 
 High for specifications and RV compatibility; Medium-High for cross-model performance. 
 Current Jackery documentation establishes the critical electrical and expansion specifications, while independent reviews support its RV-oriented physical design. We do not have standardized independent delivered-energy testing across every product on this page under the same RV load.
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 — Best Premium Off-Grid RV Power Station 
 Why We Picked It 
 The DELTA Pro 3 has the strongest all-around RV energy ecosystem in this shortlist.
 EcoFlow specifies:
 4,096Wh base capacity;
 4,000W continuous AC output;
 8,000W surge;
 native TT-30R;

 30A Anderson DC output;

 compatibility with EcoFlow’s 800W Alternator Charger;

 For an RV owner building a serious off-grid energy system, those attributes are more important than simply having the highest inverter number.

 In 240V mode, the 240V outputs are used instead.

 Weight is substantial.

 It is also more system than many RV owners need.
 If your requirement is only:
 1,000–1,500Wh/day 
 a smaller 2kWh platform can be easier to manage.
 Best For 
 Choose the DELTA Pro 3 for:
 extended boondocking;
 large daily energy budgets;
 high solar availability;
 RV owners wanting a strong DC ecosystem;
 alternator charging;
 expandable off-grid systems;
 users with legitimate 240V requirements that match EcoFlow’s output architecture.
 Evidence Rating 
 High. 
 Current manufacturer documentation is detailed, exact-model availability is active, and independent review evidence supports its RV/off-grid positioning.
 BLUETTI AC200L — Best 2kWh Portable Power Station for RVs 
 Why We Picked It 
 The BLUETTI AC200L is the most balanced option here for someone who does not need a 3.5–4kWh base battery.
 It provides:

 1,200W solar input;

 Those are unusually RV-specific attributes in a roughly 2kWh product.

 Its 1,200W solar input is also high relative to a 2,048Wh battery.
 Under idealized arithmetic:
 2,048Wh ÷ 1,200W ≈ 1.7 hours

 Load management may be necessary.
 For example:
 air conditioner + microwave + coffee maker

 The AC200L also does not provide 240V split-phase output.
 Best For 
 Choose the AC200L if:
 your calculated energy requirement is around the 2kWh class;
 your simultaneous AC load stays below 2,400W;
 native TT-30 is important;
 you want a regulated RV/DC option;
 solar and alternator charging are priorities;
 you want battery expansion without beginning with a 100-pound base unit.

 High for specifications; Medium-High for comparative performance. 
 The RV feature set is documented directly by BLUETTI, and multiple independent sources have used or evaluated the model in RV/off-grid contexts.

 BLUETTI specifically markets the Apex 300 as an RV platform, including mobile shore-power use through TT-30 and modular AC/DC integration.

 If requirements later increase, the ecosystem can add substantial battery capacity.

 campground shore power → driving → boondocking → solar charging 
 because recharge flexibility can matter as much as base battery capacity.

 The ecosystem is more complex than buying a standalone battery.
 Accessories such as:
 Hub D1;

 Independent long-term U.S. field data is also less mature than for older platforms such as the AC200L or EcoFlow DELTA Pro line.

 Choose the Apex 300 if you want an RV power platform that can grow substantially over time rather than a fixed-capacity portable station.
 It is especially attractive for:
 full-time RVers;
 large solar arrays;

 long-term boondocking;
 users planning future expansion.

 Medium-High. 
 Current manufacturer documentation is strong and the platform is specifically designed around RV/off-grid configurations, but broad independent long-duration evidence is still developing.
 Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus — Best High-Output 120/240V RV Option 
 Why We Picked It 
 The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus is the power-oriented option.
 Anker specifies:
 3,840Wh LiFePO4 capacity;
 6,000W total AC output;
 120/240V output;
 TT-30;
 L14-30R;
 up to 3,200W solar input;

 This is the model to consider when the RV requirement includes legitimate high-output or 240V loads that smaller stations cannot support.

 Strengths 
 The key advantage is 6,000W of continuous inverter output.
 That gives the F3800 Plus much greater high-load headroom than:
 AC200L at 2,400W;
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus at 3,600W;
 BLUETTI Apex 300 at 3,840W;
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 at 4,000W.
 It can also supply 120/240V through its high-power connection architecture.
 For an RV system with substantial electrical loads, that can be more useful than an extra few hundred watt-hours of battery capacity.
 Solar input is also excellent at up to 3,200W on the F3800 Plus generation.
 Important TT-30 Qualification 
 Do not assume the TT-30 port can deliver the full 6,000W inverter capability.
 Anker specifies the F3800 Plus TT-30 output at 3,000W maximum .
 Its L14-30 connection is the high-output 120/240V path and is rated up to 6,000W.
 For a normal 30A RV that only uses TT-30, this makes the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus a cleaner match to full 3,600W theoretical 30A service.
 Limitations 
 At 136.7 pounds, this is not a casually portable battery.
 It has wheels, but getting it up RV steps, into a pickup bed, or through a tight storage compartment can still require planning or more than one person.
 Its high-output capability is also unnecessary if your RV loads peak at only 1,500W.
 An independent 2026 field review praised the F3800 Plus’s power and expansion but similarly penalized portability because of its size and weight.
 Best For 
 Choose the F3800 Plus if:
 high AC output matters;
 120/240V capability is genuinely required;
 you want a very large expansion ceiling;
 high solar input matters;
 the station will remain mostly in one part of the RV rather than being carried frequently.
 Evidence Rating 
 High for specifications; Medium-High for RV-specific field evidence. 
 Current Anker documentation clearly defines the exact F3800 Plus generation and its port limits, avoiding confusion with the older F3800.
 Which Portable Power Station Is Best for a 30-Amp RV? 
 For a straightforward 30A RV connection, our first choice is the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus .
 Its TT-30 output is rated:
 120V × 30A = 3,600W 
 which matches the theoretical maximum of conventional 30A RV shore power.
 That does not mean you should intentionally operate at the limit continuously.
 You still need to account for:
 startup demand;
 battery runtime;
 converter load;
 simultaneous appliances;
 manufacturer limits.
 The other TT-30 models remain useful but differ in available output:
 BLUETTI AC200L: 2,400W total inverter
 Anker F3800 Plus TT-30: 3,000W maximum
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus TT-30: 3,600W maximum
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3: 4,000W total system output in its applicable 120V mode
 This is why comparing the plug alone is misleading.
 Which Portable Power Station Is Best for a 50-Amp RV? 
 A normal 50A campground connection can theoretically provide:
 120V × 50A × 2 legs = 12,000W 
 None of the single power stations on this page should be described as a complete 12kW replacement for unrestricted 50A campground shore service.
 Instead, identify the loads you actually need.
 The most relevant single-unit candidates for higher-power RV systems are:
 Anker F3800 Plus for 6,000W 120/240V output
 and:
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 for 4,000W 120/240V capability.
 The BLUETTI Apex 300 also provides a more advanced modular architecture that can expand into larger multi-unit systems.
 A 50A RV owner should therefore think in terms of:
 load-managed backup/off-grid power 
 rather than:
 full campground service replacement 
 unless the exact multi-unit system has been designed and verified to provide the required electrical architecture.
 Which Is Best for RV Air Conditioning? 
 Air conditioning requires two separate qualifications:
 Can the station start and run the air conditioner? 
 and:
 Does it contain enough energy to run it for the required time? 
 A 6,000W inverter does not automatically mean long air-conditioner runtime.
 Suppose an exact RV air conditioner averages, hypothetically:
 1,300W 
 for four hours.
 Energy requirement:
 1,300 × 4 = 5,200Wh 
 before other RV loads and conversion losses.
 That already exceeds the base capacity of every station on this page.
 For longer A/C runtime, expansion batteries and recharge capability become more important than maximum inverter wattage alone.
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3, Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus, BLUETTI Apex 300, and Anker F3800 Plus are therefore stronger air-conditioning platforms than a fixed 2kWh battery because they can grow into multi-kWh systems.
 The exact A/C startup and running requirements still need to be checked.
 Which Is Best for RV Solar? 
 For maximum published direct solar-input capability among the products here:
 Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus — up to 3,200W 
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 — up to 2,600W 
 BLUETTI Apex 300 — up to 2,400W 
 BLUETTI AC200L — up to 1,200W 
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus — up to 1,000W 
 However, maximum PV input is not enough to choose a system.
 You also need:
 compatible panel voltage;
 array open-circuit voltage;
 current limits;
 connector architecture;
 roof area;
 shading;
 realistic solar harvest.
 See How to Charge a Portable Power Station With Solar Panels before connecting an RV solar array.
 Which Is Best for Charging While Driving? 
 Among these picks, EcoFlow currently has the clearest high-power vehicle-charging path.
 Its 800W Alternator Charger supports the DELTA Pro 3 when used with the required custom connection hardware. EcoFlow states that it can add approximately 1kWh in 1.3 hours under its specified conditions.
 BLUETTI’s current AC200L ecosystem also supports an optional 560W alternator charger.
 A hypothetical energy comparison illustrates why this matters.
 At:
 800W × 3 hours driving = 2,400Wh idealized input 
 versus:
 100W × 3 hours = 300Wh 
 a high-power DC-DC charging system can fundamentally change how much base battery capacity an RV needs.
 Real charging power may be lower, and vehicle alternator capability must be verified.
 Is a 2kWh or 4kWh Power Station Better for an RV? 
 A 2kWh station is usually more attractive when:
 daily loads are modest;
 solar is reliable;
 the station must be moved;
 air conditioning is not a major battery load;
 the RV already has a house battery.
 That is where the BLUETTI AC200L fits.
 A 3–4kWh station is more attractive when:
 daily energy use exceeds roughly 1kWh;
 recharging is uncertain;
 you want meaningful overnight reserve;
 appliances use more AC power;
 expansion is likely.
 That is where the:
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus 
 and:
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 
 become stronger choices.
 How Expansion Changes the Recommendation 
 Base capacity is only the beginning for most products here.
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus 
 A base unit contains:
 3,584Wh 
 One HomePower 3600 Plus can support five compatible expansion batteries for approximately:
 21.5kWh total 
 according to Jackery.
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 
 Base:
 4,096Wh 
 One unit can expand to roughly:
 12kWh 
 using two DELTA Pro 3 extra batteries. Larger multi-unit EcoFlow systems can scale substantially further.
 BLUETTI AC200L 
 Base:
 2,048Wh 
 BLUETTI’s current U.S. configuration supports expansion beyond:
 7.5kWh 
 depending on compatible battery selection.
 BLUETTI Apex 300 
 Base:
 2,764.8Wh 
 The Apex platform is designed around extensive B300-family expansion and multi-unit architecture, with BLUETTI advertising system configurations reaching approximately 58kWh.
 Anker F3800 Plus 
 Base:
 3,840Wh 
 With six 3,840Wh BP3800 expansion batteries:
 3.84kWh × 7 total battery modules = 26.88kWh 
 for one expanded inverter system.
 Larger paired configurations can scale further.
 Do not buy expansion capacity you do not need.
 A modular ceiling is valuable because it gives you a path forward—not because the largest possible configuration is automatically the correct one.
 Weight Matters Inside an RV 
 Battery weight can affect more than convenience.
 Our recommendations range from roughly:
 62 pounds 
 to:
 137 pounds 
 before expansion batteries.
 Model 
 Approximate base weight 
 BLUETTI AC200L 
 62.4 lb 
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus 
 77.2 lb 
 BLUETTI Apex 300 
 83.8 lb 
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 
 113.5 lb 
 Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus 
 136.7 lb 
 That weight needs to be:
 physically accommodated;
 safely secured during travel;
 considered against RV cargo limits;
 placed where ventilation remains adequate.
 Expansion batteries add more weight.
 The best RV battery system is not one that creates a payload or storage problem.
 Don’t Ignore the RV Converter 
 If you connect the portable power station to the RV’s shore-power inlet, the RV converter/charger may activate.
 That can make the energy path:
 PPS battery → AC inverter → RV converter → RV 12V system / house battery 
 The converter itself may therefore become part of the load.
 This is one reason direct DC capability can be useful.
 It is also why a station connected to an RV inlet can consume energy faster than a simple list of visible 120V appliances suggests.
 For the full architecture discussion, return to What Size Portable Power Station Do You Need for an RV? .
 Portable Power Station vs RV House Battery 
 A portable power station and an RV house battery system are not automatically interchangeable.
 A conventional RV system may integrate:
 house battery;
 converter/charger;
 inverter;
 DC distribution;
 AC distribution;
 shore power;
 solar controller;
 alternator charger.
 A portable station packages many related functions into one device, but the electrical architecture is different.
 The right role may be:
 supplement 
 rather than:
 replace. 
 Products such as the AC200L, Apex 300 and DELTA Pro 3 include increasingly sophisticated RV/DC features, but permanent integration should still follow the exact manufacturers’ supported configuration.
 Safety and Connection Considerations 
 Do not connect a portable power station to an RV with improvised backfeeding or homemade high-current wiring.
 Before feeding the RV shore inlet, verify:
 output voltage;
 outlet limit;
 adapter rating;
 RV inlet type;
 neutral-ground behavior;
 electrical management system compatibility;
 simultaneous load.
 A physically compatible plug does not guarantee complete electrical compatibility.
 Large power stations also need to be secured during travel.
 Do not allow a 60–140 pound battery to move freely inside the RV.
 Keep cooling openings clear, follow the exact manufacturer temperature limits, and do not assume that an outdoor/RV product is waterproof.
 See the Portable Power Station Safety Guide for broader ownership guidance.
 Recall and Current-Market Check 
 Power Station Scout searched the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission recall database for the exact recommended model names during the September 11, 2026 evidence review.
 No exact-model recall notice surfaced in our searches for:
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus;
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3;
 BLUETTI AC200L;
 BLUETTI Apex 300;
 Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus.
 That is a dated search result—not a guarantee that a model has never been recalled or will not be recalled later.
 CPSC states that its online recall data is updated as new recalls and product-safety warnings are announced.
 Exact-model recall status should therefore be checked again immediately before publication and during future commercial updates.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 What is the best portable power station for an RV? 
 For a typical 30A RV, our best overall choice is the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus because it combines 3,584Wh capacity, a 3,600W inverter, native TT-30, major battery expansion, and a comparatively manageable 77-pound chassis.
 For a more advanced off-grid system with strong solar, DC and alternator capabilities, we prefer the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 .
 What is the best portable power station for a 30-amp RV? 
 The Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus is our strongest direct 30A match because Jackery rates its TT-30 outlet at 120V/30A and its inverter at 3,600W.
 The BLUETTI AC200L is the lighter alternative if your actual loads remain under 2,400W.
 What is the best portable power station for a 50-amp RV? 
 A 50A RV can theoretically access far more power from campground service than any single recommendation here supplies.
 For high-output load-managed use, look first at the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus or EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 because both support 120/240V architectures.
 Do not assume either recreates unrestricted 12kW campground 50A service.
 Is 2,000Wh enough for an RV? 
 It can be.
 A 2kWh station is useful when your RV loads are modest or when daily solar and vehicle charging replace much of the energy used.
 It may be insufficient for extended air conditioning, heavy electric cooking, or multiple days without charging.
 Is 3,600Wh enough for an RV? 
 For many moderate RV energy budgets, 3.5–4kWh is a substantial amount of storage.
 If your RV consumes:
 1,200Wh/day 
 a 3,584Wh rated battery represents roughly three days of headline capacity before losses and reserve.
 If the RV consumes:
 5,000Wh/day 
 the same battery is less than one day’s requirement.
 Which RV power station has the most solar input here? 
 The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus has the largest manufacturer-specified solar-input ceiling among our five main recommendations at up to 3,200W .
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 follows at 2,600W .
 Which is the lightest RV power station in this list? 
 The BLUETTI AC200L is the lightest at approximately 62.4 pounds .
 It also has the smallest base battery among our five recommendations at 2,048Wh.
 Which RV power station is best for alternator charging? 
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 currently has the strongest clearly documented first-party vehicle-charging ecosystem among these picks through EcoFlow’s 800W Alternator Charger.
 BLUETTI offers an optional 560W alternator charger for the AC200L.
 Can I plug my RV directly into one of these power stations? 
 Some have native TT-30 outputs designed for this purpose.
 That still requires you to verify:
 the RV load;
 station output limit;
 grounding behavior;
 converter load;
 RV electrical-management system;
 manufacturer instructions.
 Do not treat physical plug compatibility as complete system compatibility.
 Can these run an RV air conditioner? 
 Some can, depending on the exact air conditioner.
 Continuous output and startup demand must both qualify.
 Runtime then depends on the battery capacity and how long the compressor operates.
 An air conditioner can consume several kilowatt-hours during extended use, so expansion and recharging often become central to the system.
 Do I need a TT-30 outlet? 
 Not necessarily.
 You can power individual RV appliances directly from ordinary AC, USB or DC outputs.
 A TT-30 is especially useful when you want a straightforward physical connection to a 30A RV shore-power inlet.
 Is 240V useful in an RV power station? 
 Only if your actual RV electrical architecture or loads require it.
 Most conventional 30A RVs use 120V.
 Larger 50A RVs use a split-phase service architecture, but a portable power station’s 240V capability does not automatically reproduce full 50A campground service.
 Bottom Line 
 For a typical 30A RV , the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus is our best overall portable power station .
 Its combination of:
 3,584Wh battery + 3,600W AC output + native 30A TT-30 + expansion to roughly 21.5kWh + 77-pound chassis 
 creates the strongest balance of RV electrical fit, stored energy, scalability, and transportability.
 Choose the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 when you need a more capable off-grid ecosystem with 4,096Wh of base capacity, 2,600W solar input, high-amp DC, alternator charging, and sophisticated 120/240V options.
 Choose the BLUETTI AC200L when a 2kWh battery is enough and you want TT-30, RV-oriented DC outputs, expansion, strong solar input, and much less base weight.
 Choose the BLUETTI Apex 300 when you want to build a modular RV energy platform rather than simply buy one fixed portable power station.
 Choose the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus when high continuous output and 120/240V capability outweigh the considerable size and weight.
 But the product comes after the requirement.
 The correct decision sequence remains:
 RV loads → connection method → simultaneous watts → startup watts → daily Wh → recharge plan → required capacity → qualified models 
 If you do not yet know those requirements, begin with What Size Portable Power Station Do You Need for an RV? .
 Size before you buy
 Confirm simultaneous watts, daily watt-hours, startup demand, and a dependable recharge plan before choosing a model.

 Disclosure · We may earn a commission when you buy through links on this page, at no extra cost to you. As an Amazon Associate, WattRatings earns from qualifying purchases. Commissions never influence scores or verdicts — see how we rate . 
 First, the Uncomfortable Truth About 30A
 A 30A RV shore connection delivers up to 3,600W continuously, for as long as you're plugged in . A 50A connection delivers 12,000W. No portable power station replaces that. The biggest unit we track — the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 at 4,000W output and 4,096Wh of storage — can match a 30A pedestal's power for about an hour at full tilt before the tank is empty.
 Run the numbers on the loads that make an RV feel like an RV:
 Load Typical draw 1 hour of use 
 Rooftop AC (13.5k BTU) ~1,500W running, 3,000W+ start 1,500Wh 
 Electric water heater element ~1,400W 1,400Wh 
 Microwave ~1,000W ~170Wh (10 min) 
 Space heater 1,500W 1,500Wh 
 One afternoon of air conditioning is 4,500–6,000Wh delivered — more than a DELTA Pro 3 holds. So the honest framing for this guide: a power station is not shore power replacement; it's a silent, instant subsystem for everything except climate control and resistive heating. Sized and used that way, the 2kWh class is genuinely useful in an RV. Sized as a generator replacement, any unit will disappoint you.
 What a 2kWh Station Actually Does in an RV
 Here's a realistic overnight off-shore (boondocking) budget, excluding AC and heat. Model: runtime = Wh × 0.85 ÷ (watts × duty). Full assumptions in our methodology .
 Load Spec 24-hr delivered Wh 
 12V compressor fridge 60W at 40% duty 576 
 Lighting 20W × 5 hr 100 
 Phones/tablets (4 charges) 15Wh each 60 
 Laptop 60W × 3 hr 180 
 Water pump, fans, misc ~150Wh 150 
 Coffee maker, 1 pot 950W, ~160Wh 160 
 Total ~1,225Wh 
 That's ~1,440Wh of rated capacity after inverter losses — comfortably inside a 2kWh unit with about 20% margin. The 2kWh class is therefore the correct size for one full day of everything-but-climate , with solar extending it indefinitely.  Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus — best for solar-first setups
 The Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus leads the class on the two specs that matter most for RV use: a 3,000W inverter with 6,000W surge (it will start almost any single appliance you throw at it short of the rooftop AC compressor on a hot day), and 1,400W of solar input — 40% more than the other two. If your roof or ground array is large, this is the unit that can actually use it.
 Who it's for: boondockers building around solar. The 6,000W surge also makes it the safest pick if you're unsure what your RV's startup spikes look like.
 Bluetti Elite 200 v2 — best capacity-per-pound
 The Bluetti Elite 200 v2 carries the most energy in the class (2,073Wh) at the lowest weight (53.4 lbs — 8 to 14 lbs lighter than its rivals) and recharges fastest from the wall (0–80% in 70 minutes). The 2,600W/5,200W inverter covers microwaves, kettles, and induction plates with room to spare.

 When 4kWh makes sense: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 (4,096Wh, 4,000W, 113.5 lbs, WattScore 92) is the only portable unit that can briefly behave like shore power — it will run a 13.5k BTU rooftop AC, for roughly 2 hours of compressor runtime. As two full days of non-climate loads, it's excellent; as an AC solution, it's a stopgap for one hot evening, not a season.
 Who it's for: full-timers who boondock for multi-day stretches and want genuine two-day autonomy plus emergency-AC capability. At 113.5 lbs, plan a permanent mounting spot — this is installed equipment, not luggage.
 Ports: What Your RV Setup Actually Needs
 A 30A RV outlet (TT-30) on the station lets you feed your RV's existing distribution panel through your shore cord — every onboard outlet and the converter just work. The 2kWh-class units above offer RV-style output either natively or via adapter; confirm the specific model's port sheet before buying a cord.
 12V/10A regulated DC output matters more than it looks: running the fridge on DC instead of through the inverter avoids inversion losses on your single largest 24-hour load.
 High-wattage solar input ports (and their voltage ceilings) decide whether your panel array is usable at all. Check the input voltage range against your panels' series wiring, not just the wattage number.
 USB-C PD 100W ports charge laptops without waking the big inverter — small loads on the AC bus force the inverter to idle-burn watts all day.
 What to Skip
 Skip any plan that includes rooftop AC on battery (unless you're buying the DELTA Pro 3 for two-hour emergencies). The duty cycle of climate control doesn't fit portable storage economics.
 Skip electric water heating and space heating. Resistive heat at 1,400–1,500W devours a 2kWh unit in ~75–90 minutes. Propane exists; use it.
 Skip the sub-1kWh class for RV duty. A 1kWh unit is half a day of the budget above. Fine as a cab-area device charger; wrong as the house battery.
 Skip oversized panel arrays that exceed the input ceiling. 1,600W of panel on a 1,000W input is 600W of wasted purchase.
 Skip daisy-chaining cheap inverter generators "for backup" before you've measured your actual loads — most RVers who do the line-item budget find the 2kWh station plus propane covers everything but summer AC.

 FAQ
 Can a power station run my RV air conditioner?
 Only the largest units can start and run a 13.5k BTU rooftop AC (~1,500W running, 3,000W+ surge), and even then the math is brutal: a 4,096Wh DELTA Pro 3 delivers roughly 2 hours of compressor runtime. For the 2kWh class, treat AC as out of scope. Soft-start kits lower the surge barrier but do nothing about energy consumption.
 Should I plug my whole RV into the station via the shore cord?
 Yes, if the station offers a TT-30/RV output — it's the cleanest setup because every onboard outlet works normally. One caution: your RV's converter/charger will try to charge the chassis batteries from the station, which can quietly add 100–300W of draw. Switch the converter off when running from the station.
 How much solar do I need to boondock indefinitely?
 Against the ~1,225Wh/day budget above, you need to harvest ~1,450Wh/day (accounting for inverter losses). At a 70% real-world derate and 4 good sun hours, that's about 520W of panel — call it 600W for weather margin. The Explorer 2000 Plus's 1,400W ceiling gives you room to over-panel for cloudy regions.
 Is the 2kWh class too heavy to be "portable"?
 At 53–67 lbs, these are two-hand or wheeled units. In RV use that's mostly irrelevant — the station finds a home near the shore-cord hatch and stays there. If you genuinely need to carry power to a separate campsite regularly, keep a sub-10 lb unit alongside for that job.
